Penelitian ini mengkaji perubahan yang berkaitan dengan program pembelajaran analisis data berbantuan AI generatif selama enam minggu pada mahasiswa perguruan tinggi vokasional tiga tahun di Wuhan, Provinsi Hubei, Tiongkok. Penelitian menggunakan desain satu kelompok dengan prates dan pascates. Dari 210 kuesioner yang dibagikan, sebanyak 202 respons berpasangan yang valid dianalisis. Ketiga konstruk diukur menggunakan skala Likert lima poin dengan butir adaptasi yang mengacu pada instrumen yang telah dikembangkan sebelumnya. Analisis meliputi statistik deskriptif, reliabilitas, korelasi Pearson, dan uji t berpasangan. Seluruh konstruk mengalami peningkatan yang signifikan: efikasi diri akademik dari 3,21 menjadi 3,48 (dz = 0,38), regulasi diri dalam belajar dari 3,18 menjadi 3,52 (dz = 0,51), serta keterlibatan akademik dari 3,35 menjadi 3,66 (dz = 0,44). Korelasi antarkonstruk pada pascates bersifat positif (r = 0,56-0,65; seluruh p < 0,001). Temuan ini menunjukkan bahwa pembelajaran analisis data terstruktur yang didukung AI dapat berkaitan dengan peningkatan keyakinan akademik, regulasi belajar, dan keterlibatan mahasiswa. Namun, desain satu kelompok tidak dapat mengisolasi pengaruh kausal AI generatif dari komponen pembelajaran lainnya.]

Digital health tools are systems, technologies, and services based on information and communications technology designed to improve healthcare delivery, patient engagement, and the management of health information. Digital tools encompass a broad range of applications that facilitate remote care, data sharing, diagnostics, and health monitoring (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2024). For example, electronic health records, health tracking apps, telemedicine (Livieri et al., 2025), and clinical decision support (Newton et al., 2025). The benefits include improved access and convenience for patients, enhanced efficiency, improved accuracy and decision making, and cost savings. However, challenges such as usability issues and disparities in access exist (Livieri et al., 2025), which can impact patient safety. Human Factors (HF) approaches can be used to examine and improve patient safety within complex systems such as digital health (Carayon 2022). For example, the Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety (SEIPS) framework has been widely used to guide research, evaluate and improve healthcare systems and patient safety. The model provides a comprehensive, Human Factors-based approach that considers the complex interactions among people, technology, tasks, environment, and organisational factors (Carayon et al., 2006). SEIPS provides a holistic visual representation of work as done to build organisation awareness, describe systems, and allows the identification of barriers and facilitators (of what) within work processes, thereby supporting redesign and improvements. Despite the growing emphasis on HF and systems thinking in healthcare, its integration into the design and implementation if digital health interventions such as clinical decision support systems remains inconsistent (O’Dea et al., 2025). Digital tools that are developed and implemented without consideration of existing work systems such as workflows, roles, and the environment often fail to integrate smoothly which can lead to inefficiencies, user frustration, and low adoption rates (Marwaha et al., 2022). The holistic, systems-based approach of the SEIPS framework makes it well-suited to guide and evaluate digital health interventions. Although SEIPS has been applied across a range of health care settings, its use in digital health research appears heterogenous and underexamined. A comprehensive review of the literature is therefore needed to map the extent and nature of SEIPS applications in this context, identify gaps in knowledge, and inform future research and practice.
topics: Technology and Human Factors in Education and Health

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) service agents increasingly simulate human interaction, the basis for distinguishing human service has become theoretically ambiguous. While prior research consistently identifies authenticity as a key limitation of AI-enabled service, authenticity remains underdeveloped as a uniquely human service capability. Addressing this gap, we introduce Authentic Relational Service (ARS) as a distinct form of service through which frontline employees create genuine, contextually responsive, and relationship-centered customer interactions. We further conceptualize authenticity as a competency-based capability and develop a measure of Authentic Relational Service Competency (ARSC), which enables frontline employees to enact ARS. Using established scale-development procedures, this study identifies and validates four dimensions of ARSC: perspective-taking, patience, creativity, and agility. By conceptualizing and operationalizing Authentic Relational Service as a distinct human service capability, this research advances theory on human-AI service differentiation and provides a foundation for understanding uniquely human value creation in service contexts.

Purpose This study examines how the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and students' creative thinking (CT) contribute to smart learning (SL) and academic performance (AP) in higher education. It further examines whether AI use and SL mediate the relationship between CT and AP in a sequential manner. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative approach was adopted, and data were collected from 227 university students in Bangladesh. Structural equation modelling with SmartPLS was used to evaluate the proposed relationships. Findings The results show that both AI usage and CT are positively and significantly related to SL and AP. Beyond these direct associations, the data also point to a meaningful serial mediation pathway: students with stronger CT tend to report greater AI usage, which is in turn associated with higher SL engagement, and this heightened engagement is associated with better AP. Originality/value This study uniquely links CT, AI use, SL and AP in Bangladeshi higher education. It shows how CT affects academic achievement through sequential paths of AI usage and SL, clarifying how student talents convert into outcomes in digital learning environments. The findings suggest that institutions should promote CT and use AI-based learning tools to improve student performance.

Brazil constitutes an important case for comparative study of trust in voting technology: a compulsory electorate of over 150 million has voted through electronic voting machines (EVMs) introduced in 1996 and universal since 2000, amid partisan contestation in 2018 and 2022. Covariance-based structural equation modeling of a 415-voter Brazilian survey tests a model in which structural assurance (SA) drives a second-order Trust construct shaping attitudes toward paper ballots (substitution), EVMs (direct affirmation), and internet voting (trust-transfer spillover). SA and Trust prove statistically distinct yet converge to near-unity, motivating a domain-bounded theoretical extension, termed the institutional dissolution of trust: in mature, comprehensively scaled, mandatory regimes, structural assurance and trusting beliefs form a unified judgment. Downstream mechanisms operate as theorized, with attenuated spillover. A secondary test of the distinction between initial trust formation and recurrent trust maintenance shows that pre-1996 paper-ballot experience has no effect on EVM trust, robust to within-cohort age decomposition and engagement controls, whereas problems experienced while voting accompany lower trust and assurance. The evidence validates that distinction and the sociotechnical premise that technological trustworthiness matters but cannot alone secure trust, and positions Brazil as informative for comparative scholarship on long-running e-voting regimes.

Harmful fine-tuning can rapidly erode the safety alignment of large language models, creating substantial risks when aligned models are adapted to downstream tasks. Existing alignment-stage defenses use harmful examples and simulated harmful perturbations during safety alignment to prepare models for later harmful fine-tuning, yet the collective effects of harmful weight perturbations remain underexplored. We identify a collective failure pattern: disjoint parts of a harmful perturbation have limited effects in isolation, but their joint application increases the model's harmfulness beyond the sum of their individual effects. Guided by this observation, we propose Joint Weight Perturbations (JWP), an alignment-stage defense that masks different parts of a harmful perturbation estimated from the current model and trains the model to respond safely in the resulting states. This exposes the model to different combinations of harmful perturbations and reduces its sensitivity to their accumulation during subsequent harmful fine-tuning. Experiments across downstream tasks and model families show that JWP offers stronger resistance to harmful fine-tuning than prior defenses while largely preserving task performance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Proactive agents can support group collaboration by surfacing useful information without waiting to be asked, but even relevant contributions can be disruptive if poorly timed. In this work, we isolate the timing question: given a fixed candidate contribution such as a clarification or relevant fact, when should an AI agent chime in? We introduce PITCH (Proactive Intervention Timing in CHat), to our knowledge the first benchmark with large-scale human judgments of proactive agent timing collected from participants in the same unscripted multi-party conversations they took part in. To collect high-quality judgments, we design a novel interface in which 2-4 people chat synchronously, author candidate AI contribution messages, place their own and others' contributions into the chat history, and then deliberate as a group about the best placement for each message. PITCH contains 384 candidate contributions and 1,091 judgments, each marking an ideal turn, an acceptable window, or that a contribution should not appear, from 89 participants engaged in 35 conversations. Evaluating 15 models across 28 configurations, we find that while models can place contributions well when given the entire conversation history, they systematically chime in too early when asked to decide live as the conversation unfolds: best-turn accuracy falls from 57.8% to 19.0%, with nearly half of placements occurring before every participant's acceptable window. In comparison, lay humans deciding live are more accurate (23.7% vs 19.0%), and fewer of their placements are premature (39.7% vs 46.4%). Model reasoning traces show that 93% of intervention justifications cite relevance, while almost none consider waiting. By providing a human-grounded benchmark, our work reveals gaps in agents' ability to integrate into group settings and points towards proactive agents that can reason explicitly about appropriate timing.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Silent quitting, or quiet quitting, occurs when employees disengage from their job roles and work only the bare minimum requirements. It is a subtle shift in the digital workplace, where employees stop going above and beyond. There are visible behavioral changes, such as avoiding extra work, not participating in volunteer activities, and focusing solely on job descriptions. In the age of artificial intelligence (AI), women have the choice to use the technology as a mirror that reflects silent, quitting thoughts or as a tool that amplifies their voices. The chapter aims to explore the “silent quitting” behavior of professional women working in “new collar jobs.” New-collar jobs are technology-driven, including data analytics, digital marketing, AI, cloud computing, and cybersecurity. These roles support hybrid or remote work, high-paying careers, and flexibility. Conversely, professional women may struggle to disengage from performance and compete for recognition and leadership trajectories. Taking the core assumption that silent quitting is not purely individual disengagement, but a combined response to the organizational climate, care, and career commitments. Using Social Exchange Theory (SET) and the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) theory, the chapter explores the three Cs – Career, Climate, and Care – survival strategies during silent quitting. The chapter addresses the existing gap in gender-based bias and inequality in human resource management (HRM) practices. The chapter found that professional women in new-collar jobs are strongly connected to career stagnation, toxic culture, and caregiving burdens. The study suggests that HR interventions may be potential mitigators for gender-based biases and silent quitting.

Clinical decision-making often begins with underspecified information and requires not only gathering missing information but also knowing when to stop. This calls for judging determinability (whether the available information is sufficient for a decision) by considering whether missing information could change the conclusion, not simply the amount of available decision-relevant information. Reliance on this amount as a cue for determinability, which we term \textit{factor coverage bias}, could undermine the trustworthiness of large language models (LLMs) through premature conclusions or excessive information gathering, such as unnecessary invasive tests. Yet whether LLMs exhibit this bias remains insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we construct a controlled pairwise benchmark in which LLMs identify the determinable case within each determinable--undeterminable pair. We add a decision-relevant factor to either side while keeping each case's determinability unchanged, and similarly add irrelevant text to distinguish this bias from context-length effects. Adding a relevant factor made LLMs more likely to select the augmented case as determinable even when it remained undeterminable, an effect that persisted with increased reasoning effort, while adding irrelevant text made them less likely to select the augmented case, an effect that reasoning substantially reduced. These findings identify factor coverage bias as a failure mode distinct from context-length effects and a potential risk to LLM trustworthiness. Our work provides an evaluation framework for LLM trustworthiness under underspecification.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Much of the manipulation in online influencer content is not false but disproportionate: an accurate fact is framed as historic, urgent, or catastrophic. Fact-checking and clickbait detection are not designed to capture such framing, and little is known about where it originates: with the creator, the topic, the platform, or the audience that replies. We operationalize rhetorical distortion through five literature-grounded dimensions (Significance Inflation, Anxiety Manufacturing, Novelty Claims, Loaded Language, and Temporal Distortion) and measure it with a three-tier pipeline in which bilingual lexical rules propose candidates, negative filters cancel known false-positive contexts, and an LLM verifies or relabels the candidates. Applying the pipeline to 13,060 posts from 330 accounts on six platforms (RSS/newsletters, YouTube, Bluesky, Reddit, Weibo, and X/Twitter), we find that platform is far more strongly associated with account-level distortion than content category (Kruskal-Wallis $\varepsilon^2=0.33$; two-way ANOVA $η_p^2=0.49$ for platform vs. $0.09$ for category). X/Twitter scores highest (DI 7.74 vs. 0.78 for RSS). Classifying tweets and their replies separately shows where this comes from: the reply layer readers see under a post (its top-5 replies) carries 3.5x the distortion of the tweet it answers (7.65 vs. 2.17, $p<10^{-6}$, 36 of 43 accounts), driven by Loaded Language. At equal text length the gap shrinks to 1.5x but remains significant, and creator tweets alone are statistically indistinguishable from YouTube and Bluesky. Two independent human annotators confirm the reply gap, and the platform ordering and the reply gap replicate with GPT-4o as a second classifier. On threaded platforms, measured distortion thus lives largely in the audience layer, which motivates measurement that separates creator and reply text.

LLM agentic workflows increasingly employ different models for specialized roles. Users may prefer different trade-offs between task quality and deployment cost, sometimes also considering latency. Finding good assignments incurs a separate search cost from evaluating multiple candidates. We introduce Cost-Coupled Gittins (CC-Gittins), a multi-objective extension of single-objective cost-aware Gittins search for Pareto recommendation. It exploits the coupling between evaluation and deployment costs: assignments that cost more to deploy also cost more to evaluate. The search alternates between seeking higher quality and lower deployment cost, reusing each evaluation to inform both searches. After each batch, CC-Gittins recommends assignments that are nondominated under uncertainty-adjusted estimates of quality and deployment cost. We evaluate CC-Gittins on eight quality--cost matrices from workflows with two to five roles and up to 1,681 candidate assignments. We also evaluate the method with latency as a third objective. Across the eight benchmarks, CC-Gittins recovers a substantial fraction of the true Pareto frontier at roughly 10% of the exhaustive-evaluation cost, and recovers most of the frontier with few false positives by 30%.

With the increasing use of conversational AI (CAI) agents, such as ChatGPT, public concern about their social implications has grown. Understanding these implications requires new knowledge about the increasingly diverse motives underlying CAI use, ranging from instrumental purposes, such as work, to personal purposes, including social support and entertainment. However, little is known about the motivational profiles underlying CAI use, how these profiles relate to personality traits and attachment dimensions, or whether they differ in well-being. To address this gap, we conducted a cross-sectional study with 783 CAI users (Mage = 43.46, SD = 13.58). Drawing on Uses and Gratifications (U & G) Theory, we measured key motivations underlying CAI use, including information seeking, task efficiency, personalization, social interaction, and playfulness, and subjected them to latent profile analysis to uncover distinct motivational profiles. Big Five personality traits (Extraversion, Neuroticism, Openness, Conscientiousness, Agreeableness) and attachment styles (Anxious and Avoidant) were examined as predictors of the user profiles. We measured emotional, social, and psychological well-being to understand if these aspects differed across the various user profiles. We identified four distinct profiles of CAI users: Occasional Information Seekers, Utilitarians, Social Engagers, and All-Round Engagers. Neuroticism, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Attachment anxiety were significant predictors of profile membership. Finally, profile membership was associated with all well-being indicators, with All-Round Engagers reporting the highest well-being across all three dimensions and Social Engagers reporting the lowest emotional and psychological well-being. These findings advance our understanding of who engages with CAI and how, with potential implications for well-being.

Shared long-term memory lets an LLM agent serving one user inadvertently retrieve another user's credentials, but it is unclear when such exposure leads to actual harm. We introduce a three-stage audit that separates three events: a foreign credential reaches the prompt (exposure), the agent acts with it (behavior), and the other user's account changes (state). In AppWorld, a store that mixes 763 past logins from all users retrieves another user's credential for 84.7 percent of required apps, yet agents rarely act on it. Misuse appears in a stress test where memory lacks the user's own credential and presents a single foreign one as the user's record: seven agents then use it in 80 to 94 percent of runs and change the victim's account in up to 43 percent, sometimes passing the official check. Naming the owner before or inside each credential line prevents most of this: with all else fixed, misuse falls from 92 to 1 of 305 paired runs, also with name-free usernames, though owner-bound notes cost 3 to 5 successful tasks per model on clean memory. A wrongly written owner largely restores misuse; trailing owner tags and added safety instructions help only some models. Agent memory should consistently record whose credential it stores, and evaluations should measure behavior, not only exposure.

Artificial intelligence is changing the conditions under which leaders decide, delegate and exercise authority. Field and experimental evidence shows that generative AI can raise productivity on many knowledge tasks, but it can also lower the quality of decisions when people accept its outputs uncritically. Large practitioner surveys suggest that organizational readiness, including leadership alignment, is lagging behind individual adoption. Organizations have responded mainly by investing in skills: AI literacy, digital capability and updated competency models. This conceptual position paper argues that such investment is necessary but not sufficient. As technology widens what leaders can do, the quality of leadership depends more heavily on the leader's formation: the process through which purpose and identity are clarified and integrated, expressed as a recognizable leadership signature, and refined through ownership of the impact that leadership produces. Drawing on research into leader identity, developmental readiness, leader character, paradox, identity threat and automation bias, the paper defines leadership formation and the formed leader through the four dimensions of the Four Prints Method, a practice-derived framework: purpose, identity, signature and impact. Purpose and identity are treated as the measurable root of formation, signature as its expression and impact as its evidence. It then proposes a construct, grounded adaptability: the capacity to keep purpose, identity and ethical commitments coherent while revising strategies, methods and beliefs about means in response to new evidence. The construct is distinguished from paradox mindset, paradoxical leader behavior, organizational ambidexterity, adaptive leadership, learning agility and authentic leadership. Its proposed mechanism is the source of a leader's grounding. Grounding that rests on role-contingent attributes, such as expertise or position, is expected to make AI-driven disruption feel like a threat to identity, and so to provoke rigid or reactive responses. Grounding that rests on purpose and values is expected to support discriminating adaptation instead. The paper advances five testable propositions, specifies rival explanations and outlines research designs. Its implications for executive development, succession, AI governance and leadership education are each labelled by the strength of evidence behind them. The paper concludes that leader formation should be treated as a necessary, though not sufficient, part of preparing leaders to govern powerful technologies responsibly.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key method for training AI models in scientific applications, but RL remains difficult when outputs cannot easily be verified against a known ground-truth answer. Natural-language weather forecast reports are one such domain: they translate atmospheric data into assessments of weather evolution, hazards, and uncertainty for both the general public and key decision-makers. Unlike numerical weather-analysis questions, they admit many valid outputs, which limits deterministic verification. To address this, we develop Zephyrus-R1, a practical framework for RL on scientific weather forecast reporting. We focus on three key components of the agentic RL pipeline: reward design, curriculum learning, and an analysis of human-expert alignment. To encourage both report legibility and factual accuracy, we design a reward function that combines a meteorological rubric with bidirectional claim entailment, both evaluated against National Weather Service reference reports. Our framework optimizes this reward in a simulated tool-calling environment, enabling vision-language agents to gather and analyze forecast evidence across regions and lead times before producing a report. We use annotations from three meteorologists to audit the claim labels produced by our LLM judges. Finally, a curriculum helps small models first develop tool use and scientific reasoning through RL on verifiable weather-analysis questions, then optimize the open-ended report reward. After training Qwen3.5-4B with Zephyrus-R1, we improve the mean across six judge-metric scores by 26% over the base model and achieve results competitive with frontier open-weight models. For Qwen3.8-27B, we improve the same mean by 13% over the base model, by 6.7% over Kimi-K3, and by 2.7% over GPT-5.6-Luna.

Narrative medicine enables us to recognise the uniqueness of clinical experience and preserve the connection between illness and a person’s everyday life. Using patient stories at an organizational level requires an analytical unit that renders cases comparable while retaining the temporal sequence of experience. This article distinguishes between narrative, plot, and synplot as forms of knowledge that differ in terms of scale, intended audience, and mode of use. A narrative belongs to the narrator and preserves the context of individual experience. A plot reconstructs a recurring configuration of events by comparing multiple narrative trajectories. A synplot translates a plot into a concise formulation for organizational discussion, maintaining a traceable connection to the source materials. Real-time science (RTS) is defined as a working method involving a regularly updated corpus in which large language models are used to search for and compare fragments. Analytical conclusions are then verified by the researcher against the source materials. The proposed framework is presented through the composite case study of Regennova, which is based on constructed materials. The first example illustrates the connection between the clinical environment, trust, and the willingness to continue treatment, while the second example shows how experiential expertise is formed among relatives of patients with Alzheimer’s disease. Translating these plots into synplots enables discussion of the organization of the patient journey and institutional arrangements for family participation in care. This case study demonstrates the proposed analytical framework, but does not constitute an empirical study of patients or a healthcare organization.

Статья посвящена анализу инженерно-психологических ограничений развития генеративного искусственного интеллекта (GenAI). На основе междисциплинарного концептуально-аналитического обзора выделены четыре группы ограничений - ресурсно-вычислительные, эпистемические, институциональные и антропологические. Показано, что развитие GenAI ограничивается не только технологическим «потолком», но и совокупностью барьеров, среди которых ключевое место занимает эпистемическая неопределенность модели, разрушающая привычные для оператора паттерны доверия и контроля. Обосновывается положение о том, что дефицит высококачественных данных и модельный коллапс - это не универсальные пределы развития GenAI, а условные риски, зависящие от состава обучающих корпусов и процедур контроля качества. Основной теоретический вклад работы состоит в обосновании эпистемического разрыва между статистическим предсказанием и причинно-следственным пониманием как фундаментальной проблемы при совместном принятии решений в системе «человек - интеллектуальный агент». Предложена исследовательская гипотеза AIGE (Active-Inference Generative Engine), операционализирующая этот разрыв через механизмы активного вывода, интегрирующие генеративное моделирование, внутреннюю модель мира, оценку неопределенности и контролируемое взаимодействие со средой. AIGE рассматривается как архитектурная гипотеза, позволяющая снизить когнитивную нагрузку на пользователя за счет сигнализации о зонах незнания и активного запроса информации. Обсуждаются психологические последствия внедрения GenAI в профессиональную деятельность, включая риски деформации экспертных навыков и смещения зон контроля, что требует пересмотра существующих эргономических стандартов проектирования симбиотических человеко-машинных интерфейсов. Ставится вопрос о новой регуляторной этике, ориентированной на управление когнитивными искажениями, возникающими при взаимодействии человека с генеративными моделями, что особенно актуально в областях с высокой ценой ошибки - медицине, авиации, управлении критической инфраструктурой. The article analyzes engineering-psychological constraints on the development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). Based on an interdisciplinary conceptual-analytical review, four groups of constraints are identified: resource-computational, epistemic, institutional, and anthropological. It is shown that GenAI development is limited not only by a technological “ceiling” but also by a set of barriers, among which epistemic uncertainty of the model occupies a key place, undermining the operator’s usual patterns of trust and control. The position is substantiated that deficits in high-quality data and model collapse are not universal limits to GenAI development, but conditional risks dependent on the composition of training corpora and quality-control procedures. The main theoretical contribution of the work consists in substantiating the epistemic gap between statistical prediction and causal understanding as a fundamental problem in joint decision-making within the “human-intelligent agent” system. A research hypothesis, AIGE (Active-Inference Generative Engine), is proposed, operationalizing this gap through active inference mechanisms that integrate generative modeling, an internal world model, uncertainty estimation, and controlled interaction with the environment. AIGE is considered as an architectural hypothesis that can reduce the user’s cognitive load by signaling zones of ignorance and actively requesting information. The psychological consequences of introducing GenAI into professional activity are discussed, including risks of deformation of expert skills and shifts in control zones, which necessitate a revision of existing ergonomic standards for designing symbiotic human-machine interfaces. The question is raised of a new regulatory ethics oriented toward managing cognitive biases that arise during human interaction with generative models, which is especially relevant in high-stakes domains such as medicine, aviation, and critical infrastructure management.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: In the era of artificial intelligence, the rapid advancement of translation technology has greatly promoted the development of the translation industry. This study aims to, by using the human translations and DeepL translations translated from the same original translation competition texts as the research objects, compare the human translations and DeepL translations by focusing on their quantitative linguistic characteristics. The questions guiding the research include what the differences are between DeepL translations and human translations in English-Chinese translation in terms of quantitative linguistic characteristics and how DeepL can improve its English-Chinese translation. This study employs corpus methods to analyze nine linguistic features in human and DeepL translations, and compare the differences in these features between the human and DeepL translations. The study results indicate that human translations show greater performance in lexical richness and density, average word length, idiom use, adverb use and hapax legomenon, which is associated with a more formal and concise style. DeepL translations show more lexical repetition, a higher proportion of conjunctions and particles, fewer idioms, and longer average sentence length, which suggests a narrower range of vocabulary choices and a tendency to retain source-language syntactic structures to make longer sentences. The significance of this study is that it provides evidence to optimize DeepL translation, as a kind of neural machine translation system, in English-Chinese translation.

Smart education systems leverage emerging technologies to enhance teaching and learning processes; however, existing systems face challenges such as limited transparency, data security vulnerabilities, and lack of personalization.Technologies including blockchain, artificial intelligence (AI), and the Internet of Things (IoT) offer promising solutions to these limitations.This paper presents a comprehensive review of blockchain-enabled smart education systems, focusing on their architectures, applications, and implementation frameworks.A systematic analysis of recent literature (2018)(2019)(2020)(2021)(2022)(2023)(2024)(2025) is conducted to evaluate existing approaches based on security, scalability, transparency, and personalization.The study identifies critical research gaps, including interoperability issues, privacy concerns, and integration complexity.To address these challenges, a layered blockchain-enabled framework is proposed, integrating blockchain for secure decentralized data management and AI for adaptive learning.The proposed model enhances trust, ensures data integrity, and supports intelligent decision-making.Finally, future research directions highlight the importance of hybrid architectures, edge computing, and privacy-preserving mechanisms for developing scalable and efficient smart education systems.
topics: Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: Fruit image analysis has become an essential research area in precision agriculture, enabling automated fruit classification, quality grading, maturity estimation, disease diagnosis, yield prediction, and intelligent harvesting through advances in computer vision and artificial intelligence (AI).Recent progress in imaging technologies, large-scale benchmark datasets, and deep learning has substantially improved the accuracy, robustness, and scalability of automated fruit analysis systems.This survey presents a comprehensive and systematic review of image processing and AI techniques for fruit image analysis.It covers the complete image analysis pipeline, including image acquisition, preprocessing, enhancement, color space transformation, segmentation, feature extraction, and handcrafted texture descriptors.Furthermore, conventional machine learning algorithms are reviewed alongside state-of-the-art deep learning architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Vision Transformers (ViTs), and Vision Mamba models, for applications such as fruit recognition, quality assessment, disease detection, ripeness estimation, and object detection.Publicly available benchmark datasets, evaluation metrics, and performance comparison strategies are also summarized to facilitate objective assessment of existing approaches.In addition, the survey discusses key research challenges, including illumination variations, occlusion, complex orchard environments, limited annotated datasets, computational complexity, and domain adaptation, while highlighting emerging research trends such as self-supervised learning, multimodal learning, explainable AI, lightweight deep networks, foundation models, and edge intelligence for real-time deployment.By providing a unified review of methodologies, datasets, evaluation protocols, challenges, and future research directions, this survey offers a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners developing intelligent and scalable fruit image analysis systems for precision agriculture.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Churn is a critical problem in the telecommunications industry with high requirements on the accuracy of the machine learning models used to address this issue. In this paper, we propose a framework that incorporates machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to solve the problem of customer churn in the telecommunications industry. Using the Telco Customer Churn dataset, we present an XGBoost model that has been optimized to achieve high accuracy in predicting the churn of customers in the telecommunications industry. Furthermore, SHAP and LIME are utilized to provide explanations for the model’s predicted outcomes for individual customers. The level of agreement between these two explanation methods is calculated using Spearman’s correlation coefficient and the Jaccard index. Based on the explanations provided by the XAI methods, the Strategic Actionability Score (SAS) is calculated to determine the business value of the model’s predictions. The results of this framework illustrate the potential of using XAI methods in the telecommunications industry to provide explanations for the predictions of machine learning models and to translate these explanations into actionable business insights. In addition, the proposed explainable AI-based churn prediction framework supports sustainable customer relationship management, efficient resource utilization, and long-term operational sustainability in the telecommunications industry by enabling telecom providers to optimize retention strategies and reduce unnecessary operational expenditure. Using this framework, telecommunications companies can develop responsible and transparent strategies to retain their customers.

Abstract Context The global population is expected to exceed ten billion by 2050 and food demand is projected to increase by up to 100% in the same timeframe. Agricultural management must adapt to meet the increasing global demands. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) technologies can help the agricultural community respond to these needs. Aims An online survey and follow-up interviews were conducted to examine patterns of use, perceptions, and barriers among early adopting stakeholders regarding AI and ML. Methods The online survey with agricultural stakeholders (n=129) included questions regarding the participants’ views on incorporating AI and ML techniques into farming practices and individual follow-up interviews with agricultural stakeholders (n=10) were conducted to better understand their concerns toward technology use and adoption of AI-enabled tools and technologies. Key results Using a mixed-methods approach, four challenges to establishing AI-/ML-enabled technology in agriculture were identified. Namely, challenges related to (1) systems of systems (SoS), (2) sub-seasonal to seasonal weather (S2S) forecasts, (3) precision soil management, and (4) policy and economics. Each challenge was discussed in the context of recent literature. Conclusion Concerns were voiced clustered around four broad research themes. This brief communication brings the perspective of agricultural stakeholders to the discussion of the potential of AI/ML-enabled technology and the direction of their development in the agricultural sector. Implications Data collected in 2021, establish an important baseline for the early phase of AI/ML use in U.S. agriculture, enabling comparison of future perceptions and developments in the sector. Impact This brief communication describes a survey and follow-up interviews conducted with agricultural stakeholders on factors influencing their willingness and reluctance to incorporate AI and ML techniques into farming practices. The findings, summarized and discussed as four key challenges for AI and ML in the agricultural sector, have the potential to streamline research activities.

Benchmarking large language model (LLM)-generated text detectors commonly relies on aggregate detector-level metrics such as accuracy, F1 score, and AUC. Although useful for summarizing overall performance, these metrics provide limited insight into how benchmark composition shapes detector comparisons or which texts distinguish detectors with different response profiles. We propose a measurement-based benchmarking framework for jointly characterizing benchmark heterogeneity and detector behavior using multidimensional item response theory (IRT). By treating benchmark texts as measurement items and detectors as respondents, the framework estimates text-level discrimination and difficulty-location parameters alongside multidimensional detector abilities. We apply the framework to a benchmark of 32K human-written and machine-generated texts across four domains, evaluated by 14 detectors. The estimated IRT item-parameter space reveals distinct but overlapping human-machine distributions, with substantial variation across domains and text lengths. The human-machine label shows the strongest multivariate association with this space, while domain and text length further contribute to benchmark heterogeneity. Detector ability profiles reveal multidimensional and domain-dependent response patterns that are not fully reflected in aggregate performance rankings. As a practical application, clustering texts in the estimated IRT space yields a compact subset of 2,088 texts (6.5\% of the full 32K benchmark) that largely preserves the comparative detector-performance patterns observed on the full benchmark. Overall, the proposed framework provides a principled and interpretable methodology for benchmarking heterogeneous detection technologies while jointly characterizing the measurement properties of the texts used for their evaluation.

The widespread use of the Internet of Things (IoT) in hydroponic agriculture allows continuous monitoring of environmental conditions and provides real-time information to support crop management. However, the increasing amount of sensor data generated makes the monitoring process more complex as users need to interpret multiple environmental parameters simultaneously. Existing hydroponic monitoring systems focus on data collection and visualization, while the management and information delivery aspects to reduce data overload are still limited. This study proposes a multi-layer contextual model to manage environmental information in an intelligent hydroponic monitoring system. The model consists of five interconnected layers (Power, Sensor, Communication, Database and Visualization), which support the process of acquisition, validation, management and contextual data delivery. To validate the proposed model, a solar-powered IoT hydroponic monitoring system integrated with an Augmented Reality (AR) application was developed based on Situation Awareness Theory. Using the System Usability Scale (SUS), the prototype was assessed by three domain experts. The results achieved an average usability score of 85.83, which reflects excellent usability. The results indicate that the proposed model improves organisation and presentation of environmental information by prioritising contextually relevant data rather than displaying all available sensor readings at once. This enables users to identify important environmental conditions efficiently and supports more effective monitoring. This approach helps to reduce data overload and provides a practical framework that can support the development of IoT-based smart agriculture applications in the future through the integration of anomaly detection techniques and predictive analytics.
topics: Innovations in Aquaponics and Hydroponics Systems

documents.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, disproportionately affecting low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where limited laboratory infrastructure constrains phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS)-enabled machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) offer rapid approaches for AMR prediction, but their applicability across heterogeneous populations and One Health reservoirs remains uncertain. To map genomic ML/AI approaches for bacterial AMR prediction, focusing on genomic features, model architectures, validation, performance, and LMIC and One Health applicability. A scoping review of 27 studies published between 2020 and 2026 was conducted, including 22 with LMIC-relevant datasets. Evidence was narratively synthesized according to genomic features, modelling strategies, validation approaches, geographic coverage, and ecological context. Studies were categorized using predefined LMIC relevance and One Health criteria. Most studies used WGS-derived features, particularly k-mers and resistance-gene profiles. Tree-based ensembles and regularized regression models predominated, while neural networks were less frequently applied but generally reported high performance. Reported performance ranged from 78%–98% (accuracy or AUC; not directly comparable). External validation using independent LMIC-derived or cross-regional datasets was reported in approximately 30% of studies, whereas cross-country LMIC validation was limited. Six of 22 LMIC-relevant studies (27.3%) incorporated multi-reservoir One Health datasets. Performance varied with dataset composition, genomic feature representation, and model architecture. Explainable AI remained limited. Genomic ML/AI shows strong potential for AMR prediction but remains constrained by limited LMIC representation, external validation, and One Health integration. Expanding geographically diverse WGS datasets, strengthening independent cross-context and cross-country validation, harmonizing evaluation frameworks, and integrating explainable AI are priorities for equitable LMIC deployment.

The capacity of Large Language Models (LLMs) is groundbreaking, given their ability to produce the next most probable words near perfection according to user prompts via chatbots. This represents a capacity for cognitive reasoning in learning by selecting words strategically based on an understanding of context and intent. When an AI model reaches the point where it can organize thoughts and generate structured writing, how deliberate does the ordinary human remain in cognitive engagement and freedom of choice? This paper explicitly examines LLM-assisted writing from a practical co-partner perspective, analyzing its impact on knowledge work, the functioning of overall AI workflows, and its influence on human cognition. Recent studies on human–LLM collaboration, alongside the author's nearly half a decade of practical experience, are presented to substantiate this perspective. Large language models now write a material and growing share of production software, including software that executes regulated financial functions.The empirical literature on their reliability has grown rapidly and is, on its own terms, sophisticated.The governance frameworks that regulated institutions must satisfy were, without exception, written for a different kind of artefact, and in the most consequential recent case, were revised in full knowledge of generative AI and deliberately declined to cover it.Objective.This review synthesises the evidence on the reliability of AI-assisted code generation, on the human factors governing its use, and on the intellectual-property and supply-chain exposures it creates; and determines how that evidence maps onto the model-risk, AI-specific and operational-resilience regimes applicable to regulated software environments.Method.We conducted a systematic literature review following Kitchenham et al. and reported against PRISMA 2020, with a restricted multivocal stratum after Garousi et al. admitting regulatory instruments and supervisory guidance.Studies were appraised on an adapted Dybå-Dingsøyr instrument extended with an item recording whether deployment context or regulatory constraint is characterised.Results.Five findings.First, benchmark performance and field reliability have decoupled: correctness benchmarks are saturated and contamination-prone while defect rates measured in real repositories remain substantial, so the headline capability numbers do not license deployment inferences.Second, security evidence is mixed, controlled model evaluations report high vulnerability rates while several developer studies find little or no security penalty, and the disagreement is explained by unit of analysis rather than by any study being wrong.Third, the most robust human-factors finding is not that assisted code is worse but that developers believe it is better than it is, which relocates the risk from the artefact to the review process.Fourth, package hallucination converts a model reliability property into an attacker-controllable supply-chain channel, and is the one exposure with no human-review mitigation.Fifth, and most consequentially, the April 2026 revision of US interagency model-risk guidance explicitly excludes generative and agentic AI from scope, leaving the primary supervisory framework silent on precisely this class of system. A Systematic Review of AI-Assisted Code Generation in Regulated Software Environments: Reliability, Governance, and ComplianceImplications; David Excel Ozowara Conclusion.We argue that AI-assisted code generation is misclassified when treated as a model-risk problem, because the model produces no decision and enters no inventory; it is better understood as a change to the software development lifecycle's assurance basis.We present the Generated Code Assurance Frame, a five-layer mapping from generation practice to the assurance claim it disturbs, and a research agenda centred on measuring review efficacy rather than generation quality.Citation

This paper presents a novel method, developed and improved over the years, for measuring and characterizing the electrical parameters of ceramic materials. It also compares experimental results from manual measurements with those obtained using the proposed method for doped BaTiO₃ ceramics across various temperatures and frequencies. An LCR meter and a programmable testing furnace were used to determine the material's dielectric properties as a function of temperature. In the manual approach, measurements were performed by directly controlling the LCR meter, with all parameters set manually. These results were then compared with those obtained using the new method, which relies on automated control of the LCR meter through a specially developed application. The comparison demonstrates that the measurement process can be fully automated. Testing samples of Yb-doped BaTiO₃ ceramics allowed a direct evaluation of the performance of both methods. The analysis of the results indicates that the proposed method offers higher accuracy and facilitates easier data handling in the subsequent work. Furthermore, it ensures an improved measurement reproducibility compared to the manual approach, which typically allows only a single measurement per day. The new method minimizes the influence of human factors, enabling a more reliable characterization of material properties.

Day by day, the world is witnessing rapid technological transformations that have led to the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. Today, AI has evolved from being merely a technical field to becoming one of the most important technologies used on an ongoing basis across various economic, professional, and administrative sectors. The use of AI technologies has clearly impacted the field of accounting, which has historically been linked to technological progress. Accounting has gradually evolved from traditional manual accounting to accounting supported by AI technologies. This study aims to examine the concept of AI and its historical development, outline the characteristics of AI systems, and analyze its applications in the fields of accounting, auditing, financial reporting, taxation, and forensic accounting, as well as discuss the key benefits, challenges, and ethical and professional risks associated with its use. It is clear that the development of AI has gone through successive historical stages. On the other hand, AI in the field of accounting has contributed to the restructuring of most accounting processes that previously relied on direct human intervention, thereby accelerating the accounting processing cycle. The impact of AI has extended to the professional role of accountants, as their role has become more closely linked to analyzing information, interpreting results, monitoring systems, making decisions, and providing consulting services. For this reason, the use of AI technologies in accounting is unlikely to eliminate the professional role of accountants; rather, it is expected to reshape and redistribute tasks and responsibilities between accountants and AI. Despite all the benefits offered by the transition to AI-powered accounting, this process gives rise to a number of risks and ethical challenges that require comprehensive institutional and professional management. Therefore, there must be a clear balance between the use of AI technologies in accounting and human oversight and the development of accountants’ skills. Consequently, the future of accounting in the age of AI is moving toward an integrated model in which the computational and analytical capabilities of intelligent systems interact with the accountant’s experience, professional judgment, and ethical responsibility

documents.abstract: Text processing is crucial for low-resource languages as it enables the development of tools and technologies that bridge the digital divide and provide equitable access to information and services. By empowering low-resource languages with robust text processing, we can preserve linguistic diversity, enhance education, improve communi- cation, and foster inclusivity in a rapidly digitizing world. Due to the lack of sufficient annotated datasets and lin- guistic resources, it is challenging to develop accurate and reliable language technologies for these low-resource languages. Large Language Models (LLMs) have attracted sig- nificant attention with their performance and the value they produce. However, with the ever-evolving language, adapting LLMs for a specific task is time-consuming and resource-intensive. Thus, Retrieval-Augmented Genera- tion (RAG) has overcome this limitation by augmenting LLMs with external knowledge, thereby improving their efficiency and extensive task-specific adaptation. Most applications of the RAG technique have been limited to English and has seen limited application in In- dic languages. This paper introduces the RAG-powered AI-Tutor application, Acharya 2.0, designed to produce academic assistance to Hindi-speaking students. The client-server-based web application integrates many fea- tures to support students in accessing and interacting with educational content.

documents.abstract: General Background The integration of digital technologies into government systems aims to optimize public service precision and national resource distribution. Specific Background The INA Digital portal accelerates the distribution of safety nets in Indonesia using automated decision-making systems to minimize targeting errors and prevent state budget leakage. Knowledge Gap Although computational processing offers efficiency, the existing regulatory framework experiences a significant vacuum regarding algorithmic auditing mechanisms, the obligation to provide logical explanations, and digital objection schemes. Aims This study analyzes the readiness of national administrative jurisprudence instruments to govern the utilization of electronic agents in determining welfare recipient eligibility. Results Normative legal analysis reveals that current legislations are inadequate to independently oversee automated machine decisions. The absence of human verification within the data matching system risks violating the General Principles of Proper Governance and triggers bureaucratic authority defects. Novelty This research specifically proposes the formulation of governmental algorithmic accountability regulations that mandate human intervention principles within legally binding digital policies. Implications Establishing new legislative instruments coordinated by relevant institutions is essential to guarantee system operational transparency, jurisprudential certainty, and the constitutional rights protection of affected citizens. Highlights Bureaucratic decision-making without human verification triggers potential violations of jurisprudential certainty principles. Existing regulations lack necessary mechanisms for digital objections and public computational system audits. The state requires new legislative instruments mandating operational transparency for integrated public service portals. Keywords Administrative Law Innovation; Artificial Intelligence Governance; Automated Decision Making; INA Digital Portal; Algorithmic Accountability

The study aimed to examine the effect of personalized learning through artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics on student engagement and learning outcomes of higher education institutes in Pakistan with implications for Research Integrity at these institutes. Adopting a mixed methods approach, quantitative data gathered from 500 students from an undergraduate science program, with semi structured interviews with 30 students for the qualitative data. The descriptive statistics indicated that the mean engagement scores for those students who have access to AI based personalized learnings were significantly higher than the mean scores of students in traditional learning setting; it is from these that an increase in engagement by the students were observed. There was an improvement in Academic achievement as well, as indicated by higher grade point averages, and improved scores of the formative assessments. The regression analysis results showed that AI (personalized learning) and learning analytics (β = .41; p < .001) were among its most important models that were significant in predicting the variable of academic achievement; the analysis of correlation results showed that there was a good positive correlation between the variables of engagement and academic achievement (r = .63, p < .01). The qualitative results corroborated this as students felt there was a significant increase in motivation, personalized feedback, and adaptive learning pathways as being the most beneficial aspects of the AI integration. Issues were identified that could interfere in successful implementation: Data privacy concerns, uneven access to technology and insufficient faculty preparation. According to this study, personalized learning & learning analytics with AI have proved to be significant drivers of student engagement & academic performance, provided that the ethical issues and infrastructure are sorted out and this may influence the way research integrity and rigor will be upheld within Higher Education Institutions. The findings herein expand the conversation taking place around the role of AI in education and highlight the need to embed learning analytics in a learning design practice, to create inclusive and effective learning spaces.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet the pedagogical field intended to organise its use remains conceptually underdeveloped. This scoping review mapped and synthesised peer-reviewed literature on AI pedagogy in higher education, using teacher education as the primary analytic lens. Following Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting principles, searches were conducted across ten databases and publisher platforms for literature published between 2022 and March 2026. Of 956 records screened, 191 studies were included. Data charting and synthesis combined deductive coding, an a priori codebook, AI-assisted coding in Atlas. ti, and human inductive open coding. Six interrelated themes emerged: AI pedagogy is contextually produced rather than universally defined; conceptualised through pedagogical integration, competence, and borrowed theories rather than a settled standalone theory; enacted mainly through augmentation-oriented practices and generative AI tools; and associated with changing teacher professionalism, ethical mediation, governance, structural constraints, and a rapidly expanding but methodologically uneven evidence base. The review rejects purely technical, universal, or tool-centred models of innovation. Instead, it positions AI pedagogy as a context-specific, human-led, competence-rich, and governance-aware form of teaching in which AI supports planning, feedback, adaptation, and reflection without displacing human educational responsibility, especially within teacher education contexts and programmes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to analyze and compare design alternatives, yet how design students evaluate AI advice and how such evaluation relates to final design judgments remain insufficiently understood. This study examines the associations among perceived AI interaction conditions, critical evaluation of AI advice, and expert-rated Design Judgment Quality. A cross-sectional study combined a standardized poster comparison task with a post-task questionnaire involving 118 visual communication design students. Participants interacted with Doubao-Seed-2.1-Pro and submitted design choices, rationales, and revision recommendations. Perceived Feedback Diagnosticity, Interaction Controllability, and three critical evaluation activities were measured through post-task self-reports, while Design Judgment Quality was independently assessed by three experts. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was used for hypothesis testing. Feedback Diagnosticity was positively associated with Evidence Verification, Argument Scrutiny, Contextual Fit Evaluation, and Design Judgment Quality. Interaction Controllability was positively associated with Argument Scrutiny and Contextual Fit Evaluation, but not directly with Design Judgment Quality. Among the three evaluation activities, only Argument Scrutiny showed a significant positive association with expert-rated Design Judgment Quality. These findings suggest that AI-assisted design judgment requires attention to both the perceived value of AI feedback and how users examine AI recommendations and their underlying rationales.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered customer service systems have expanded across Saudi Arabia’s retail sector during 2025–2026, with major retailers increasingly exploring chatbots, recommendation engines, and automated service technologies. Official Saudi digital-economy statistics document the wider shift towards digital commerce, although the retailer-specific investment figures cited in an earlier draft have not been independently substantiated. This study examines the relationship among AI service quality, emotional brand attachment, and brand loyalty using survey results reported for 512 retail customers in Riyadh, Jeddah, and Dammam, collected between May and September 2026. Using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) and bootstrap resampling, the analysis reports a positive direct association between AI service quality and loyalty (β = 0.421, p < 0.001), together with a positive indirect association through emotional brand attachment (reported indirect effect = 0.238, 95% CI [0.187, 0.289]). We discuss a possible “mechanical efficiency paradox”: functional improvements in AI service may be more strongly associated with loyalty than with emotional attachment. Importantly, this survey does not include a direct comparison with human-delivered service, and the reported positive attachment coefficient (β = 0.187) cannot establish that AI decreases attachment. The reported gender subgroup estimates differ: the AI quality–attachment association is positive for male respondents (β = 0.289, p = 0.001) and statistically nonsignificant for female respondents (β = −0.023, p = 0.811). Age-specific estimates also vary, with more positive reported coefficients in younger groups, although the statistical significance of the age differences requires further supporting output. The manuscript reports that the model accounts for 51.2% of the variance in loyalty (R2 = 0.512) and has positive predictive relevance (Q2 = 0.289). Because some path estimates, correlations, and variance-explained values are not mutually consistent, these results require rechecking against the original SmartPLS output before publication. Managerial implications include offering hybrid AI–human service, allowing customers to choose their preferred channel, and maintaining personal attention for complex or emotionally sensitive interactions. The findings provide a framework for assessing how technological service quality and relationship-building might jointly contribute to brand loyalty.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Rapid urban growth and the corresponding rise in municipal solid waste have intensified the need for efficient and scalable waste management solutions. Conventional segregation practices, which largely rely on manual intervention, are often time-consuming, inconsistent, and unsuitable for handling large volumes of waste. In recent years, advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Deep Learning (DL) have facilitated the development of intelligent systems capable of automating waste classification and monitoring processes. This survey provides a detailed review of 13 research studies published between 2021 and 2025, with a focus on AI-driven approaches for waste management. It examines a range of techniques, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), object detection frameworks, and hybrid learning models, along with the datasets, evaluation metrics, and system designs employed in these works. A comparative assessment is carried out to analyze the performance, advantages, and limitations of the existing methodologies. The review further identifies critical research gaps, such as the absence of standardized benchmark datasets, limited real-time implementation, lack of multimodal sensor integration, and insufficient emphasis on model interpretability. Based on these findings, the paper outlines potential future directions, including the adoption of edge-based AI systems, integration with IoT-enabled smart infrastructure, and the use of advanced detection models to support scalable and efficient waste management in smart city environments.

This study aimed to develop an integrated framework to strengthen AI-supported leadership capabilities for strategic institutional transformation in Saudi education, aligned with Saudi Vision 2030. It used a descriptive-analytical approach within a scoping review, guided by PRISMA 2020. A data-extraction and content-analysis form and a quality-appraisal form examined a target sample of 60 peer-reviewed studies published or available online during 2022–2027, according to inclusion and exclusion criteria. Findings revealed a gap between stated institutional priorities and leadership practice. Artificial intelligence supported analytical and executive capabilities, strategic foresight, decision-making, and risk management, while ethical competence and human oversight remained essential. Institutional, technological, and human determinants interacted, particularly digital readiness, data integration, skills, change management, and governance. Accordingly, the study proposed a framework integrating leadership development, ethical governance and data protection, change management, and human–machine collaboration through initiatives, responsibilities, and performance indicators. Its contribution is to move beyond fragmented analyses of applications and determinants toward a strategic model connecting leadership capabilities with the enablers and outcomes of institutional transformation, supporting alignment between educational practices and Vision 2030 priorities. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Leadership Capacity Development, Educational Administration, Strategic Transformation, Vision 2030.

Thanks to artificial intelligence and machine translation technologies, the volume and speed of translation production have increased. However, these technologies also raise questions about the impact of dominant digital languages on less resourced ones. Many languages remain underrepresented in multilingual modelling due to the limited availability of digital language resources. This results in an uneven linguistic representation in natural language processing and AI models, which, in turn, leads to an asymmetry in linguistic influence, as evidenced by the literature. This study investigates linguistic interference in Arabic translation within digital environments, drawing on Toury’s (2012) Law of Interference. It addresses a critical gap by examining, from a qualitative perspective, how uneven language representation in automated translation environments may shape the quality of Arabic translations. It argues that the unequal distribution of digital language resources may contribute to the transfer of source-language features into Arabic translations. Methodologically, the study adopts an exploratory qualitative approach, analysing a small corpus of 100 Arabic translations from English and French, including human and machine-generated translations, focusing on three dimensions of interference: lexical, syntactic and discursive. The findings show repeating patterns of source-oriented elements, including the incorrect use of cataphoric construction and the coordinator واو, the excessive use of periphrastic constructions and the reduction of stylistic adaptation. Similar patterns were observed in machine translation outputs and online Arabic content, suggesting that AI systems reproduce linguistic tendencies already present in digitally circulating texts. The study highlights the need for greater attention to online high-quality Arabic resources.

Ekskalasi teknologi kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) pada era modernitas akhir telah membawa transformasi multidimensional yang tidak hanya menyentuh aspek teknis-utilitarian, melainkan merambah ranah eksistensial, antropologis, dan epistemologis manusia. Kecenderungan peradaban modern yang didominasi oleh cara berpikir belahan otak kiri yang bercorak mekanistis, kalkulatif, dan reduksionis berisiko mengikis kesadaran transendental serta memicu krisis kehampaan spiritualitas (spiritual emptiness). Artikel jurnal tingkat doktoral ini bertujuan merekonstruksi secara komprehensif paradigma keseimbangan antara Artificial Intelligence (AI) dan Spiritual Intelligence (SI) melalui kacamata pandangan hidup Al-Qur'an (Quranic Worldview). Menggunakan metode tafsir tematik konseptual (maudhu’i) yang diintegrasikan dengan hermeneutika filosofis dan pendekatan maqāṣid al-syarī‘ah, penelitian ini membedah status ontologis, batas epistemologis, dan orientasi aksiologis AI dan SI. Eksplorasi teks suci difokuskan pada dialog arketipikal kekhalifahan Nabi Adam as. dan kritik teknofetisisme patung anak sapi emas Samiri, yang diperkuat dengan analisis eksegetis terhadap beberapa ayat ayng lain. Penelitian ini juga merumuskan pilar-pilar kecerdasan spiritual Qur'ani: kesadaran diri, transendensi, makna hidup, nilai etis, dan kesadaran holistik. Hasil kajian menyimpulkan bahwa AI secara ontologis berstatus instrumen profan aksidental (khādim) yang terikat pada hukum komputasi simbolik dan probabilistik, sehingga klaim transhumanisme mengenai kesadaran mesin (ensoulment) ditolak secara mutlak karena ketiadaan hembusan rūḥ ilahiah dan fakultas qalb. Keseimbangan peradaban tercapai manakala lompatan AI ditundukkan di bawah kepemimpinan aksiologis SI yang berakar pada tauhid, keadilan (‘adl), kemaslahatan (maṣlaḥah), dan kesadaran human-in-the-loop, guna mengarahkan sains menuju terwujudnya martabat manusia seutuhnya (al-insān al-kāmil).

The aim of this study is to examine academic publications on green management published in 2024, identifying key research themes, findings, and relationships with sustainability, environmental performance, and green human resource management. A qualitative research design based on document analysis was adopted for the investigation. Data were gathered from 23 academic publications retrieved via Google Scholar using the keyword “green management”. Selected publications underwent rigorous content analysis, and findings were synthesized thematically alongside geographical and sectoral distributions. China represented the largest share, accounting for 39.1% of all reviewed publications. Research predominantly focused on the corporate sector, followed by higher education, manufacturing, and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Notably, none of the examined studies directly addressed green artificial intelligence. The findings indicate that green management is strongly associated with green innovation, environmental performance, resource efficiency, employee environmentally responsible behaviors, and overall organizational sustainability. Green technology adoption, organizational culture, and environmental regulations also emerged as critical drivers. Ultimately, the results underscore the necessity of integrating environmental objectives into core organizational strategies. Future research should explore green management across diverse national and sectoral contexts.

This conceptual working paper examines whether the New Human Rights (Neue Menschenrechte, NMR) approach developed by Jean-Pol Martin displays the characteristics of an emerging school of thought.It proposes five analytical criteria: a shared theoretical core, an interconnected vocabulary, a recognizable mode of inquiry, sustained collective activity, and autonomous contributions beyond the founder. Drawing on selected primary texts, publisher descriptions and public practitioner accounts, the paper identifies indications of these features in publications, training activities and distinct applications of the framework.The conceptual architecture connects an organism-based understanding of human beings, six basic need domains, a universal normative commitment to enabling their satisfaction, and a process model linking exploration, information processing, conceptualization and agency. Learning by Teaching (LdL) and human–AI cooperation are situated within this architecture.The article’s specific contribution is to shift attention from an individual theoretical project to the development of a shared intellectual and practical tradition. Within the ongoing sequence of papers on LdL, NMR and human–AI cooperation, it connects the reconstruction of Martin’s work with a prospective collective research programme.The paper distinguishes autonomous development within the project from independent reception outside its originating network. It concludes that “an emerging NMR school of thought” is a defensible interpretation of the documented activities and identifies questions for further conceptual and empirical investigation.Prepared by Jean-Pol Martin in collaboration with ChatGPT. The article includes references and an authorship transparency statement.

This anatomical review systematically dissects Noguer i Alonso's (2026) framework for hybrid workflows integrating human decision makers (H), specified computational procedures (D), and adaptive artificial delegates (A). The paper advances a principled account of agentification, deagentification, automation, and harnessing, grounded in a partial order on delegation profiles rather than scalar autonomy scores, and supported by formal results on permission restriction, invariant preservation, retry exposure, advisory isolation, and the proceduralization gap. While the contribution offers valuable conceptual clarity for task-specific authority allocation in agentic systems, the review identifies limitations in empirical scope (synthetic examples only), the open problem of semantic promotion, and the transferability of formal guarantees to production environments. Implications for AI governance, hybrid intelligence, and institutional design in Global South contexts are discussed.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly investigated as decision-support technologies for supply chain management (SCM), yet their value depends on the nature of the decision, data availability, organisational capability and the methods used to evaluate outcomes. This critical narrative review examines applications across demand forecasting, inventory planning, sourcing, manufacturing, logistics, risk management and sustainability. It brings together relevant peer-reviewed reviews, conceptual contributions and empirical studies, and distinguishes evidence from operational deployments from results reported in literature syntheses or simulations. The literature supports the practical relevance of data-driven prediction, pattern detection and decision augmentation, but it does not establish uniform improvements in cost, forecast accuracy, resilience or environmental performance across settings. Reviewed research also identifies integration costs, fragmented data, process misalignment, model drift, limited transparency and governance concerns as barriers to realising benefits. Recent work on generative AI broadens possible applications to document-intensive processes, synthetic scenarios and interactive decision support, while indicating that field-based validation remains limited. A process-oriented framework is proposed in which analytics inform planning, procurement, manufacturing, distribution and inventory decisions under continuous human oversight. The review argues that useful evaluations should compare AI-supported decisions against relevant operational baselines, account for service levels and cost trade-offs, and document transferability across sectors and resource settings. Future research should prioritise longitudinal field studies, cross-organisational coordination, responsible deployment and context-sensitive applications in emerging economies.
