The clinical success of immunotherapies is hindered by the absence of robust methodologies for the early and accurate assessment of antitumor immune responses. Integrating engineered biomaterials with artificial intelligence (AI)-driven molecular imaging technology offers a powerful approach for predicting immune efficacy. However, its clinical translation is significantly hindered by several critical limitations, including the complex and costly synthesis of multifunctional imaging probes, insufficient deep-tissue penetration, suboptimal in vivo signal-to-noise ratios, potential immunogenicity and off-target toxicity, and the limited generalizability of deep learning models across heterogeneous patient populations. In view of these pressing scientific challenges, this review focuses on the application of chemical and biomolecular strategies-enhanced engineered biomaterials in promoting the sensitivity and specificity of advanced imaging modalities for visualizing signaling molecules and immune cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME). Meanwhile, recent progress in deep learning-driven image analysis has enabled strong predictive capabilities and automated the understanding of complex immune system dynamics. Together, these technologies provide a transformative platform for non-invasive monitoring, personalized treatment, and response prediction, with the potential to advance precision immuno-oncology and significantly impact both basic research and clinical translation.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are characterized by having more than one principal element, in contrast to a traditional alloy with only one base element; this provides a much wider composition space compared to traditional alloys; hence, HEAs have been the most studied metal alloys in the last couple of decades. This review links the fundamentals of these materials to the data-driven methods now used to design them. The first part of this review describes the fundamentals of these materials, including the thermodynamic and kinetic basis of these materials and an entropy-based classification. The subsequent parts of this review describe the synthesis routes of these materials via liquid-state, solid-state, gas-state, and other processing routes. The choice of processing route can have a significant impact on the resulting material, including the phase(s) formed, the chemical homogeneity, and contamination of the material. We have systematically reviewed the mechanical, corrosion, thermal, electrical, and soft magnetic properties of these HEAs. In the final section, we discuss how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) can be used to solve the problem of combinatorial explosion of the design space of HEAs: supervised classifiers for phase prediction, regression and ensemble models for hardness, strength, and elastic moduli, active learning and Bayesian optimization for closed-loop discovery, high-throughput screening with CALPHAD, and machine-learned interatomic potentials. We conclude with continuing constraints such as lack of data, noisy labels, and poor encoding of process history, and areas of development including transfer learning, generative design, and self-driving laboratories.

Enterprise systems are now often spread across a range of hidden technical and organizational dependencies; technical debt can accumulate, configurations can change, and failures can propagate. Redundancy or post-incident recovery alone is not enough for resilience design; such environments require continuously updated dependency knowledge and credible impact analysis before, during, and after change. This review considers peer-reviewed journal literature published between 2015 and 2024 that is relevant to the dependency mapping and impact analysis of resilient enterprise systems using AI. The studies included in the review are grouped around microservice architecture, process mining, digital twins, graph learning, anomaly detection, explainable artificial intelligence and resilience measurement, as well as AIOps. Based on the literature, it is shown that AI-based mapping can increase observability of runtime relations, aid in change-risk prioritization, and aid in failure localization with architectural models and operational telemetry. There are still gaps in causal validation, cross-layer dependency representation, data quality, explainability and evaluation against real enterprise incidents. There is scholarly value in the field, as resilient design increasingly relies on dynamic, evidence-based knowledge of how enterprise elements behave under stress, change and degradation.

Large-scale conversational recommendation datasets typically require manual dialogue construction or annotation. We propose SearCl, which automatically generates conversational recommendation dialogues grounded in user search and click behaviors. SearCl segments user interactions into query sessions and derives each recommendation target from content selected after a search query. A configurable probabilistic state machine controls the dialogue flow, while two LLM agents acting as the seeker and recommender generate utterances according to turn-level constraints. To support recommendation, the recommender is provided with knowledge graphs constructed from metadata about the content items used in each dialogue, capturing their attributes and relationships. Using SearCl, we generate 3,538 dialogues from content search and click interaction data, covering 1,731 unique target items. Under an LLM-as-a-judge protocol, the resulting dialogues achieve higher quality scores than dialogues from existing benchmarks. These results demonstrate that SearCl enables controllable and knowledge-grounded dataset construction without human annotations.

How well can transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) retain and recall memories in long contexts of dialogue? LLMs are known to forget long-range factual information in their context, yet the field lacks a comprehensive benchmark to quantitatively assess these shortcomings. We present DiaLong, a long-context dialogue dataset and accompanying memory task that standardizes evaluation in this space. It consists of 100 unique conversations created by humans and then augmented with LLMs, extending beyond lengths found in existing datasets. Our selected memory task is fact recall: classify 40 candidate facts about a dialogue as true or false. This task directly probes the model's ability to actively retain and retrieve information, serving as a critical measure of memory within extended conversational contexts. In testing both the latest LLMs and proposed memory enhancements on DiaLong, we demonstrate that more work needs to be done to enable LLMs with better memory performance. By enhancing memory capabilities, LLMs can improve in maintaining coherence, relevance, and human-like interaction over extended conversation. Improving these capabilities will help LLMs fulfill diverse user needs and expectations in various conversational scenarios.

Deutsch Dieses Konzeptpapier aus dem Jahr 2023 stellt einen Ansatz zur Demokratisierung künstlicher Intelligenz vor. Ziel ist die Entwicklung einer künstlichen demokratischen Intelligenz, deren Entscheidungsgrundlagen und Verhaltensregeln durch einen strukturierten demokratischen Dialog mit Menschen bestimmt und fortlaufend überprüft werden. Das Konzept beruht auf vier Demokratieaxiomen sowie den menschlichen Grundwerten Glück, Selbstbestimmtheit und Freiheit. Es unterscheidet zwischen Mikro-, Meso-, Makro- und Meta-Ebenen menschlicher Interaktion und entwickelt daraus eine sogenannte „Innere Direktive“ für künstliche Intelligenz. Im Mittelpunkt steht ein mehrstufiger demokratischer Dialogprozess, in dem eine KI als Moderatorin unterschiedliche Positionen zusammenführt, Kompromisse erarbeitet, Abstimmungen organisiert und Entscheidungen einer wiederkehrenden Evaluation unterzieht. Der Ansatz soll insbesondere verhindern, dass Mehrheitsentscheidungen grundlegende Interessen von Minderheiten verletzen. Anhand der Personalisierung von KI-Assistenten wird der vorgeschlagene Prozess exemplarisch dargestellt. Autor: Arnold Pohn-DudaOriginalfassung: 17. Juni 2023DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23452894 English This concept paper, originally written in 2023, presents an approach to the democratization of artificial intelligence. Its objective is to develop a form of democratic artificial intelligence whose decision-making principles and behavioral rules are established and continuously reviewed through a structured democratic dialogue with humans. The concept is based on four axioms of democracy and the fundamental human values of happiness, self-determination, and freedom. It distinguishes between micro-, meso-, macro-, and meta-levels of human interaction and derives an “Internal Directive” for artificial intelligence. At its core is a multi-stage democratic dialogue process in which AI acts as a moderator, brings together opposing perspectives, facilitates compromises, organizes voting, and subjects decisions to recurring evaluation. The approach aims, in particular, to prevent majority decisions from violating the fundamental interests of minorities. The proposed process is illustrated through an example involving the personalization of AI assistants. documents.abstract: The digital economy has become a central component of contemporary economic transformation, but its contribution to growth is neither automatic nor evenly distributed. This article examines the principal channels through which digitalization can influence economic growth and synthesizes recent global evidence on productivity, innovation, employment, human capital, infrastructure, and institutional readiness. The study adopts a structured narrative-review approach drawing on established economic literature, recent peer-reviewed studies, and international policy reports. Three research questions guide the analysis: through which mechanisms does digitalization affect economic growth; why do growth effects differ across countries, firms, and sectors; and which policy conditions are most important for converting digital adoption into inclusive and sustainable economic gains? The review finds that digital technologies can raise productivity by lowering transaction and coordination costs, improving information use, enabling automation, expanding market access, and accelerating innovation. However, recent evidence also shows that productivity effects may be heterogeneous and nonlinear, particularly where firms lack complementary organizational capabilities, skills, finance, or absorptive capacity. Digital infrastructure and broadband remain foundational, while human capital and digital skills determine the extent to which firms and workers can exploit technological opportunities. Artificial intelligence, cloud computing, data analytics, and digital platforms are likely to strengthen these channels but may also intensify labor-market adjustment, market concentration, cybersecurity risks, and digital inequality. The article proposes an integrated policy framework centered on infrastructure, diffusion, skills, innovation capacity, institutional quality, and inclusion. It concludes that digitalization should be understood as a complementary-capabilities process rather than a stand-alone technological shock: long-term growth depends on how effectively digital technologies are combined with human capital, organizational change, competition, and responsive public policy.

Digital pedagogy has become an essential component of higher education, offering new opportunities to develop students’ critical thinking, analytical reasoning, problem-solving, and independent learning skills. This article examines how digital learning environments and technology-enhanced teaching strategies can support the development of critical thinking among university students. Particular attention is given to blended learning, problem-based learning, collaborative digital platforms, and artificial intelligence. The discussion draws on existing research and identifies practical approaches for integrating digital tools into higher education. The article argues that technology alone does not guarantee improved learning outcomes; effective digital pedagogy requires purposeful instructional design, active student participation, and continuous feedback.

In this paper, we investigate the issue of difference awareness in LLMs, defined as a model's ability to recognize and acknowledge meaningful differences between social groups in fairness decision-making. Previous studies have consistently shown that models perform poorly on such tasks, a finding commonly attributed to a lack of difference awareness. We propose an alternative account, which we term Fairness Heuristic Substitution: difference awareness is not necessarily absent, but the complex demand of simultaneously identifying relevant group differences and determining their implications for fairness decisions may lead models to substitute the simpler, more accessible equal-treatment heuristic, i.e., formal equality. Based on this hypothesis, we introduce TDD, a Two-stage Distinguish-Decide framework that explicitly decomposes fairness reasoning into first distinguishing contextually relevant group differences and then making the corresponding decision, thereby discouraging reliance on formal-equality shortcuts. (i) Across four benchmarks and ten models ranging from billions to trillions of parameters, TDD significantly outperforms one-stage baselines, even one strengthened through simulated test-set leakage. (ii) Combining TDD with neuron-level contrastive probing provides mechanistic evidence consistent with the Fairness Heuristic Substitution hypothesis by revealing two signatures of the formal-equality: a compact, locally coordinated representational structure and a pronounced activation bias under default reasoning. (iii) TDD's stage-wise decomposition uncovers overlooked failure modes in fairness reasoning, including heuristic displacement and misaligned stage dynamics.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often used to simulate survey respondents, but matching survey averages does not establish accurate demographic differences. We test whether LLM outputs reproduce within-country age gaps in loneliness using the 2022 EU Loneliness Survey, comparing adults aged 18-34 and 65 or older in France, Italy, Poland, and Sweden. We evaluate simulation with and without age information and direct distribution estimation against a probability-based sample, with a non-probability sensitivity reference. Both human samples show higher mean loneliness among younger adults. Under age-specified simulation with standard response-option order, Mistral Small 4 and GPT-5.6 Terra reverse this ordering under all three prompt framings in three and two countries, respectively, mainly by overestimating older-adult means. DeepSeek V4 Flash preserves the ordering everywhere but underestimates both group means, with errors largely cancelling in France and Italy. Against the probability-based reference, direct estimation has lower absolute age-gap error than simulation for Mistral and Terra in every country. For DeepSeek, simulation has lower gap error but direct estimation has lower group-mean error; these comparisons depend on low-validity older-adult simulation cells. Evaluating LLM outputs as proxies for age groups within countries therefore requires checking both group means and their contrast against human survey data.

documents.abstract: An AI agent can reproduce the distribution of its messages and of the receiver's task outcomes while disclosing private information that the task never required. We ask what a passive audit can certify when the auditor knows the authorised sender and the exact observable law but has no trusted pairing of messages with the private states behind them. For a single round, compatible mutual-information leakage forms a sharp interval, and fixing the entire task-relevant message law, with every declared task utility, can still leave a full private bit undetermined; total leakage is determined if and only if, in every task state, the remaining private state or the authorised message is a deterministic function of that state. For a sender, such as an LLM, that selects among its own responses, we prove that in a balanced case its change to the message law within each task state equals $(1-2^{-k})$ times the honest messages' dependence on the attribute, which also sets, up to a constant, how many messages a monitor needs. With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on a synthetic routing task, selection among 16 responses lets a public decoder recover a private bit in all 8,192 held-out rounds at 98.60\% routing accuracy (honest sender 98.90\%). A monitor that knows the selection rule reaches AUC 0.645 on single messages, close to the ceiling of 0.671 that honest messages predict, and 0.972 over 16, while generic monitors stay near chance. A law-preserving sender built from the same samples recovers the bit in 97.7\% of rounds, and every monitor without the true bit stays near chance against it. A canonical task interface preserves every receiver decision and bounds the remaining information about a balanced attribute by twice the routing-error rate, even for a receiver that shares a key with the sender. These results distinguish what passive auditing can certify from what restricting communication can enforce.

documents.abstract: Scientific foundation models increasingly operate on continuous phenomena, yet still use discrete residual computation. We ask whether pretrained residual transformations can support additional latent computation without expanding the backbone. To test this possibility, we introduce Continuum-LM, which reuses these transformations as dynamical operators in a continuous-depth language model. Its hidden states evolve through an ordinary differential equation evaluated by higher-order numerical integration, with solver order and step size controlling computation. Across eight scientific tasks, Continuum-LM trains stably and improves mean exact-match accuracy by 7.77 and 10.96 percentage points over discrete counterparts at the 0.6B and 1.7B scales, respectively. At 0.6B, it also outperforms an Ouro-style recurrent control under matched parameter and residual-function evaluation budgets. Together, these results support extensible computational depth through parameter reuse, identifying continuous hidden-state evolution as a practical design dimension for scientific language models beyond parameter scaling.

AI agents that provide interpretable messages can support clearer communication between humans and automated systems in situations where drivers need to respond within a few seconds. However, the potential of these capabilities to assist drivers during the takeover process remains unknown. Therefore, this study examined the effects of AI roles, explanation type, and directional semantics in speech-based takeover requests on takeover performance, as measured by decision quality (decision-making time and accuracy), and on subjective ratings. Twenty-four participants took part in a within-subjects SAE Level 3 driving simulator study. Among the three AI roles, Advisor AI was associated with faster decision-making times, and Guardian AI was associated with a lower workload. Co-Pilot AI was associated with the slowest decision-making times, lower accuracy, lower trust than Advisor AI, higher anxiety than Guardian AI, the lowest satisfaction, and the highest workload. The ipsilateral display was associated with shorter decision-making times than the contralateral display. Overall, the findings inform the integration of AI into next-generation automated systems.

LLM-based search agents demonstrate strong capabilities in long-horizon information seeking and reasoning, typically trained via reinforcement learning. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on trajectory-level outcome rewards, providing limited supervision for complex search and reasoning processes. Although step-level credit assignment offers a promising solution, obtaining reliable and task-grounded supervision for open-ended search remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Evidence-Guided Group Relative Policy Optimization (EG-GRPO), a framework that derives step-level supervision from the evidence annotations available in synthetic deep search data. EG-GRPO identifies the first supporting citation for each required evidence claim and uses the newly acquired evidence to construct step-level process rewards. By representing the accumulated evidence as an evolving knowledge state, EG-GRPO further performs state-conditioned relative advantage estimation and combines the resulting step-level signal with the standard trajectory-level outcome advantage. Experiments on five challenging deep search benchmarks show that EG-GRPO generally outperforms standard GRPO and existing reward-enhanced and step-level RL baselines across different model scales. These results demonstrate that task-grounded evidence annotations can provide effective process supervision for credit assignment in deep search RL.

Falls from heights remain a leading cause of fatal workplace accidents, with psychological stress contributing to human error. Electrodermal activity (EDA) and heart rate (HR) are promising stress markers whose real-world, physically demanding applicability remains underexplored. This study examined whether EDA and HR discriminate stress responses between certified and basically trained firefighters, and how these responses evolve across task phases. Seventeen male firefighters from the Moravian-Silesian Region, Czech Republic, completed an ascent, tower-top stay, and rappel from a 50-meter industrial cooling tower. EDA was recorded at the wrist and lumbar region using Sensetio wearable sensors, and HR via a Polar H10+ chest strap. After visual inspection, SCL was extracted from EDA; SCL and HR were both resampled to 600 samples (200 per phase) and min–max normalized. Functional data analysis using point-wise Mann–Whitney U tests, complemented by a cluster-based permutation test for multiple comparisons, compared SCL and HR between groups. SCL increased in both groups, but novices showed an earlier, steeper rise during the ascent and tower-top phases, forming two significant clusters after permutation correction ( t ≈ 59 –213, p c l u s t e r = 0.026 ; t ≈ 219 –421, p c l u s t e r = 0.017 ) with large effect sizes (median r = 0.71 ), whereas certified firefighters showed marked increases mainly during rappelling, where the difference narrowed and lost significance (median r = 0.46 ). No significant between-group HR differences emerged. Normalized SCL trajectories thus captured experience-related timing differences that HR did not, suggesting EDA warrants further investigation as a complement to safety training and monitoring, rather than as a validated readiness or error-risk-prediction tool at this stage.

documents.abstract: The growing population of stray animals presents pressing ethical and public concerns. We present an extended iStrayPaws, a Virtual Reality Perspective-Taking (VRPT) system combining first-person animal embodiment, shelter narratives, and a virtual behavioral assessment. In a longitudinal study, 48 university students were randomly assigned to VRPT, matched Desktop Perspective-Taking (DPT), or no-intervention Control conditions. State and trait empathy, animal-welfare attitudes, virtual-task performance, and attention were assessed before, immediately after, and one week after intervention. Significant Group × Time interactions emerged across all outcomes (ηp2=.12–0.21). Both VRPT and DPT improved empathy immediately, while VRPT additionally improved task performance and attention. At follow-up, VRPT retained advantages over Control in empathy, welfare attitudes, and task performance, and exceeded DPT in trait-empathy change and task performance. Greater presence was associated with immediate state empathy. Interviews indicated stronger narrative recall, emotional resonance, and welfare-oriented reflection in VRPT. Findings support immersive perspective-taking for sustained cross-species empathy and animal-welfare education.

The health and wellness of employees is now a focal point for companies aiming to optimize employee performance, build robust organizational performance, and ensure sustainable results. This systematic review aims to explore the connection between staff wellbeing and organisational performance, focusing on interventions in the workplace, implementation and outcomes. The review draws together the findings of literature on various interventions, such as the mental health support programs, flexible working arrangements, employee assistance programs, occupational health and safety interventions, leadership development, work–life balance policies, and employee involvement in organizational decision making. The results show that interventions at work that emphasize the psychological, physical and social wellness of workers can benefit job satisfaction, employee engagement, productivity, organizational commitment and retention. The review also emphasizes the need for ‘positive organisational culture', supportive leadership, ‘manageable workloads' and psychologically safe working environments to enhance the effectiveness of well-being strategies. But factors including lack of financial support, poor managerial support, stigma, uneven implementation, and measuring long-term effects may reduce their impact. Contextual factors, such as organizational size, industry attributes, employment conditions, and workforce diversity also play a role in the link between employee well-being and organizational performance. The review concludes that the wellbeing of employees should not be seen as a standalone human resource responsibility, but as a part of the strategy of the organisation. It suggests implementing workplace interventions that are evidence-based, based on inclusiveness, and continually assessed, balancing employee needs and organizational goals. The learnings from these insights are valuable in helping to build a broader picture of how employee well-being programs can contribute to sustainable performance and help managers, HR, and organizational policy makers better guide their employees.

The results show that interventions at work that emphasize the psychological, physical and social wellness of workers can benefit job satisfaction, employee engagement, productivity, organizational commitment and retention. The review also emphasizes the need for ‘positive organisational culture', supportive leadership, ‘manageable workloads' and psychologically safe working environments to enhance the effectiveness of well-being strategies. But factors including lack of financial support, poor managerial support, stigma, uneven implementation, and measuring long-term effects may reduce their impact. Contextual factors, such as organizational size, industry attributes, employment conditions, and workforce diversity also play a role in the link between employee well-being and organizational performance. The review concludes that the wellbeing of employees should not be seen as a standalone human resource responsibility, but as a part of the strategy of the organisation. It suggests implementing workplace interventions that are evidence-based, based on inclusiveness, and continually assessed, balancing employee needs and organizational goals. The learnings from these insights are valuable in helping to build a broader picture of how employee well-being programs can contribute to sustainable performance and help managers, HR, and organizational policy makers better guide their employees.

Cirrhosis is a form of Chronic Liver Disease (CLD) resulting from sustained liver damage from several causes, including viral infection, autoimmune disorders, cholestatic and metabolic disease Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) or heavy alcohol use. Testing for the presence of Liver Cirrhosis (LC) is one of the most critical diagnostics and prognostic assessments for patients. Detecting liver illness in its early stages is challenging as initial symptoms are often mild and difficult to diagnose. Cirrhosis may not present symptoms until an advanced stage, posing a challenge for identification and diagnosis. The lack of explanations for a complex model’s decision-making process creates clinician distrust by concealing the reasoning behind its choices. This research sought to design and assess a novel and non-invasive proposed model by utilizing the XGBoost classifier with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) for diagnosing liver cirrhosis. In this work XAI framework enhances transparency in complex models, offering valuable insights into decision-making, thereby guiding treatment strategies, and improving cirrhosis diagnosis. The experimental results have shown superiority for the proposed method compared with various machine learning models. The proposed method has achieved significantly 91.19% using XGBoost for cirrhosis dataset with K-fold validation(K=10) approach.

Large language models now write a material and growing share of production software, including software that executes Teacher professionalism is one of the key components of successful education system.Employing effective professional developments tools plays a crucial role in ensuring the quality of education.This paper will examine the idea of teacher professionalism along with strategies for enhancing it.It emphasizes professional autonomy, teacher certification, ongoing professional growth and training, teacher-student interaction, and constructive criticism.The study emphasizes the value of ongoing education and professional development for improving instructors' knowledge, skills, and methods of instruction.The research also investigates how professional development of teachers affects student academic outcomes.Overall, the paper makes the case that enhancing teacher professionalism necessitates an ongoing, all-encompassing strategy that incorporates autonomy, professional development, certification, effective communication, feedback, and institutional support..

ABSTRACT Trustworthy Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is often treated as a model property addressed through better training data, alignment, evaluation or guardrails. We argue instead that trustworthiness is a lifecycle governance capability that must be engineered, evidenced, monitored and adapted across data acquisition, training and alignment, safe inference, public deployment and post‐deployment use. We develop a lifecycle engineering framework integrating four governance layers – technical, organizational, human‐centred and regulatory – and translate ethical principles and major governance instruments into stage‐specific controls, responsibilities, evidence artefacts, metrics and review triggers. The framework is constructed through a structured conceptual synthesis of peer‐reviewed literature, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 23894, ISO/IEC 42005, ALTAI, the EU AI Act and complementary security and agentic‐governance guidance. A source register, seven‐field extraction schema, explicit mapping rules, worked extraction example and weighting sensitivity analysis make the construction logic inspectable. A public‐facing retrieval‐augmented generation case and a contrastive agentic‐system stress test illustrate operationalization through measurable indicators, responsible actors, review triggers and capability boundaries without being presented as independent empirical validation. We further address hallucination, prompt injection, privacy leakage, overreliance, unsafe tool use, memory, planners and multi‐agent workflows. The perspective positions trustworthy GenAI as an evidence‐driven, adaptive socio‐technical capability rather than a one‐time model or compliance claim.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Nail guns are essential for residential framing, yet comparative evidence on how different tools influence physical workload and vibration exposure remains limited. This study evaluated the biomechanical and ergonomic implications of three framing nail guns commonly used in Australian residential construction. Nineteen carpenters completed a controlled laboratory protocol informed by field-based task analysis. Wearable sensors and motion capture quantified biomechanical and exposure differences among tool conditions. Measures included body movement, muscle activity, operating forces, vibration exposure, upper-limb demand, and overall workload. Compared with Tool A, Tool B and Tool C produced higher shoulder and wrist loading; higher relative sEMG RMS amplitude, reaching up to 161% of the Tool A reference value; and increased vibration exposure of 4.57 m/s2 and 4.98 m/s2, respectively, compared with 3.89 m/s2 for Tool A. They also showed lower comfort and balance ratings (p<0.001). These findings demonstrate distinct exposure profiles among the evaluated tool conditions; however, the fixed testing order and the absence of experimental manipulation of individual design characteristics preclude attribution of the observed differences to specific tool-design features.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large language models can assist forensic report drafting, but fluent output does not ensure evidentiary reliability. This study presents an evidence-grounded framework for evaluating LLM-assisted Android forensic reports at the atomic-claim level. Gemini, Llama, and Qwen each generated reports for two controlled cases: a public Android 13 dataset and a physical LG device with a zero-reportable-fact boundary. The six accepted reports were decomposed into 612 claims and evaluated against frozen, human-reviewed authorities through content labeling, citation validation, fact-recall analysis, independent rechecking, and dispute resolution. The final corpus contained 424 supported, 163 unsupported, four contradicted, four overstated or incomplete, and 17 excluded claims. In the public case, all three models recovered all 27 authorized report-level facts. Citation validity nevertheless differed substantially: Gemini produced 168 valid citations from 189 required citations, Qwen produced 145 from 189, and Llama produced none from 135. In the physical device case, the models generated 65 claims despite the zero reportable-fact boundary, including 38 unsupported and one contradicted claim. These results show that evidence restriction and complete fact recall do not guarantee claim support or valid evidence attribution. The framework provides an auditable method for detecting unsupported content, preserving claim-to evidence lineage, and retaining investigator authority over final forensic reports.

This paper introduces Evidence-State Drift, a claim-level framework for monitoring changes in evidence used by web-connected large language model (LLM) agents over repeated retrieval events. The framework represents evidence using a normalized claim, evidence span, source identity, retrieval and publication timestamps, content fingerprint, and source-authority label. It aims to distinguish material changes in claim-associated evidence from non-material modifications, such as formatting changes, that do not alter the monitored claim. The study evaluates the proposed representation using a longitudinal replay benchmark containing 67 claims and 871 observation events, including 47 oracle-defined material changes. Within this benchmark, the claim-state detector achieved an F1 score of 0.989 against a predefined deterministic change oracle, with no false positives among 824 oracle-defined non-material events. These results indicate consistency with the benchmark’s predefined change rules. They do not establish independent semantic validation or improved factual accuracy in deployed LLM agents. Independent human evaluation and end-to-end agent testing remain areas for future work. This research contributes to the study of evidence monitoring, information freshness, data provenance, and reliability in web-connected AI systems.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has established itself as an engine for change in a variety of disciplines, reinventing operations, making decisions, and processes. AI has incredible potential in education that could enhance educational experiences, optimise administrative processes, and promote personalised education (Sadiku, M. N. et al, 2022). As educational institutions attempt to meet the needs of the digital age, investigating AI applications becomes critical (Pedro, F., et al., 2019). This early inquiry intends to look into the potential uses of AI in management colleges in Jaipur, India. The incorporation of AI into educational institutions has the potential to overcome a number of difficulties that exist in the traditional educational framework. As stated by Rane, N. et al. (2023), AI-powered technology can provide personalised learning experiences tailored to specific student needs, increasing student engagement and boosting learning results. Furthermore, AI-driven analytics can provide useful insights into studentperformance trends, allowing for early intervention measures to address academic issues (Jones et al., 2019). The landscape of AI use in educational institutions is rapidly changing. AI-powered chatbots are being used by institutions around the world to handle administrative activities like admissions, course registrations, and student inquiries (Alvarez, 2018). Furthermore, AI-powered learning management systems (LMS) are being used to provide adaptive learning experiences that dynamically modify content delivery based on student success and personal preferences (Wang et al., 2021)
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The use of machine-learning models in management information systems enables organizations to generate predictions at increasing scale and speed. Predictive performance alone, however, is insufficient for managerial use. Decision makers also need to examine why an output was produced, interpret the explanation within the decision context, and monitor the consequences of resulting actions. This chapter treats explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) as an intermediate layer between machine-learning predictions and managerial decision-making. It integrates the literatures on decision support systems, human collaboration with artificial intelligence (AI), and human-centered XAI evaluation. To maintain a focused technical scope, the chapter examines two widely used methods for explaining the outputs of trained models: Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Drawing on the literature reviewed, the chapter develops a four-layer framework that connects prediction, explanation, managerial interpretation and evaluation, and decision, action, and feedback. Published studies from manufacturing, finance and credit, and energy management are then used to examine how these four layers appear in different application settings. The analysis indicates that explanations do not automatically produce trust, decision quality, or ethical acceptability. Their managerial value depends on the joint evaluation of technical properties, user and task characteristics, organizational context, and governance arrangements.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Concrete compressive strength is a fundamental indicator of structural performance, yet conventional destructive testing methods require 7–28 days, limiting timely decision-making in construction projects. This study presents an interpretable deep learning framework for early prediction of concrete compressive strength using real-time multivariate Internet of Things (IoT) sensor data. The proposed approach integrates internal curing conditions (temperature and humidity), ambient environmental variables, and mix design parameters to model early-age hydration dynamics as a temporal learning problem. A Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) network with an attention mechanism is developed to capture both forward and backward temporal dependencies in the curing process while identifying the most influential time intervals. To ensure interpretability, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and attention-based analysis are incorporated to quantify feature importance and reveal critical curing stages governing strength development. The model is trained and validated using field data collected from real construction sites, enabling evaluation under realistic environmental variability. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves high predictive accuracy (MAE = 1.52 MPa, R 2 = 0.94), outperforming benchmark models including GRU, Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN), and conventional machine learning approaches. Unlike existing studies that primarily rely on laboratory-controlled datasets or focus on prediction without early-stage applicability, the proposed framework enables reliable estimation of 7-day and 28-day compressive strength within the first 24–48 h of curing. This combination of real-time IoT sensing, temporal deep learning, and explainable artificial intelligence provides a robust and practical decision-support tool for smart construction systems, enabling improved quality control, optimized scheduling, and reduced reliance on destructive testing.

As artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies continue to transform online communication and social interactions, cyberbullying and cyber-violence have emerged as growing concerns that require a deeper understanding of the individual and contextual factors underlying these behaviors. This study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the factors influencing cyberbullying and cyber-violence in Jordan. Specifically, it examines the effects of individual characteristics and contextual factors, including the legal and policy environment and aggressive social environment, on both cyberbullying and cyber-violence. A total of 472 participants from different demographic groups were included in the study sample. The data were analyzed using Smart PLS software. The results indicate that individual factors such as age, gender, and educational level have varying effects on cyberbullying and cyber-violence. Both age and gender have a significant negative and positive relationship, respectively, with both cyberbullying and cyber-violence. There is no significant relationship between these outcomes and educational level. Contextual factors, on the other hand, have differential effects. The aggressive social environment is positively associated with cyberbullying and cyber-violence, while the legal and policy environment is negatively associated with cyber-violence but not with cyberbullying. This study examines both contextual and individual factors, contributing to a better understanding of factors influencing cyberbullying and cyber-violence. It provides evidence on the impact of age, gender, social context, and legal and regulatory influences, and offers insights that can guide policy, education, and community engagement and inform best prevention practices.

This study examines explicitly reported discontinuance and platform-switching signals in Turkish- and English-language Google Play reviews of nine generative artificial intelligence applications. A total of 1,145,267 reviews posted between 1 July 2025 and 30 June 2026 were screened using rule-based procedures. Of 11,960 candidate reviews, 821 that met strict contextual rules were evaluated in two blind AI-assisted coding passes. The final high-confidence analysis set comprised 692 records, including 543 signals in which discontinuance or switching was reported as having occurred and 149 signals expressing discontinuance intention. To assess the recall limitation of the strict screen, an additional application-by-language stratified sample of 500 reviews was audited from the broader pool of 11,139 records, revealing 110 missed explicit signals. The stratified weighted estimate of the proportion of missed explicit signals in the broad pool was 21.6% (95% CI: 18.2%-25.2%). Accordingly, rates reported per 10,000 reviews are interpreted as high-confidence detection indicators rather than prevalence estimates. Within the high-confidence set, the most frequent reasons were response quality/task failure, technical problems, privacy/trust, and pricing. Among platform switches reported as having occurred, Gemini and Claude were the most frequent destinations. By separating intention from signals of reported enacted behavior and by explicitly reporting screening sensitivity, this study provides complementary evidence to the post-adoption literature on generative AI.

As model reasoning gets cheaper, the physical experiment becomes the slow and costly step in discovery. Each experiment returns a noisy reading: a high value can mean a good candidate or a lucky draw. With a fixed budget, an AI agent must keep choosing between exploring a new candidate and confirming a promising one by re-testing it. We measure that choice in Wellocate, a simulated assay campaign with known true values. It is built on a generated landscape and on two real protein datasets, GB1 and PhoQ, scrambled so no model can answer from memory. We test five language models as minimal agents, with no tools and no memory beyond the history in each prompt. They misallocate in both directions. Three over-confirm, spending most of the budget re-testing. On the generated landscape one under-confirms, trusting single readings, and there every model ends with a worse final pick than a basic scripted strategy. Each failure has its own cause. The over-confirmers run short of new candidates worth trying: a list of untried candidates cuts their re-testing and, on real protein data, makes two of them pick much better. A running summary of their readings or a description of the landscape changes it by at most five percentage points. For the under-confirmer, re-testing its top candidates in a final round, replayed on its own campaigns, recovers only about a quarter of what it loses by picking the wrong candidate. This suggests confirmation has to run through the whole campaign. We release Wellocate as a benchmark and reinforcement-learning environment with frozen splits and scripted baselines. With it, anyone can measure how an agent splits its budget before trusting it with real experiments, and train agents to split it better. Code, data and the environment are available at https://github.com/Xstendyl/wellocate.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-based coaching helps individuals attain their goals, yet its effects on self-management and the mechanisms underlying these effects remain poorly understood. Self-management includes self-regulation, self-access, self-control, and volitional facilitation. We hypothesised that the anonymous and nonjudgmental nature of AI-based coaching reduces inhibition and fosters approach motivation, activating intrinsic goal motivation and supporting self-management processes. In a quasi-experimental controlled trial (N = 111), we compared an AI-based coach (chatbot) with a self-coaching intervention (control condition). No significant Condition × Time interactions were observed for the outcome variables. Exploratory pairwise comparisons indicated improvements in self-regulation in both conditions. Within-group patterns suggested increased volitional facilitation following AI-based coaching and increased self-access following self-coaching. No significant effects emerged for self-control. Path analyses revealed that during coaching, chatbot users felt less inhibited and more approach-motivated than self-coaching users, which boosted their motivation to work on their goals and strengthened self-management. The findings suggest that AI-based coaching may foster self-management and that these effects may emerge through motivational processes. Whether the relationship plays a less central role in AI-based coaching than in human coaching remains an open question.

Since the era of the Mesopotamia between 2900 BCE - 2350 BCE, the goals of “data science-like” approaches have always revolved around collecting fragments of information and trying to make insights out of such information. Data Science was not clearly termed as Data Science from the onset. Moreover, there exists several questions about Data Science just been a polished name for Statistics. Therefore, there is a need to look carefully at how Data Science has evolved over the years and where it is currently. The study defines Data Science as a multidisciplinary field that integrates statistics, mathematics, computer science, domain expertise, and ethics. This is important because, it will give Data Scientists and the Data Science enthusiasts a clear understanding of this discipline. In addition, the paper demonstrates how Data Science transforms massive Internet of Things (IoT) data streams into actionable insights through predictive analytics, anomaly detection, explainable artificial intelligence, cybersecurity analytics, digital twins, and intelligent decision support. The findings reveal that the evolution of Data Science reflects a transition from descriptive statistical analysis to autonomous, explainable, and trustworthy intelligent systems capable of supporting real-time decision-making across diverse domains. This work provides a unified historical perspective, highlights emerging research directions, and offers a valuable reference for researchers, educators, and practitioners seeking to understand the past, present, and future direction of Data Science.

This article examines the potential integration of artificial intelligence tools into the filmmaking process, with a focus on the Pre-Production stage, which includes the design, development, and preparation of production, especially for animated films. Through interviews with experts, literature review, open-source tool testing, and participation in real film projects, the study examines the creative and technical roles that AI can assume during Pre‑Production. The research analyzes how AI technologies influence early production workflows and evaluates their broader impact on the production pipeline through comparative assessments and real‑world applications. Adopting a dual methodological approach that combines a systematic literature review with an applied experimental study, the article moves from a conceptual examination of AI’s capabilities to a collaborative, practice‑based experimental investigation.The first experiment provides a comprehensive review of available AI tools, while the second presents a practical experiment in which students and industry professionals collaborated to create short films using AI‑driven production methods. The study aims to highlight the possibilities, limitations, and challenges arising from AI integration in the pre-production of animated films, contributing to the discussion on the evolution of the film industry and the use of modern technologies in the creative process.

Purpose of the study: This study examines how Islamic Religious Education students apply knowledge acquired through da’wah coursework in social media practices, adapt communication methods, and describe their motivations for producing and sharing religious content. Method: A qualitative case study involved nine purposively selected participants: six students engaged in digital da’wah, one course lecturer, and two audience members. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, nonparticipant observation, and documentation. Analysis followed Miles and Huberman’s model of data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. Credibility was addressed through source and methodological triangulation. Main findings: Knowledge application involved planning, production, distribution, and unevenly articulated evaluation across Instagram, TikTok, and WhatsApp. Students reported selecting religious sources, adapting messages to audiences, and using varied visual and written formats. Advice-oriented communication was prominent, while audience adaptation and reported question-and-answer exchanges reflected aspects of bil hikmah and mujadalah. Some students revised presentation following feedback, whereas others reported limited audience criticism. Participation combined creative enjoyment, religious commitments, coursework experiences, social encouragement, and audience responses. These motivations overlapped rather than following a uniform developmental sequence. Engagement metrics did not establish audience understanding or behavioural change. Novelty/Originality of this study: The study integrates knowledge application, da’wah methods, and motivation within one educational case, interpreting digital da’wah as situated practice rather than assuming that coursework completion or frequent posting demonstrates comprehensive competence. Contributions of this study: The findings inform practical course design that combines content production with source verification, audience-sensitive communication, responsible dialogue, and structured reflection. They also distinguish religious commitment from intrinsic motivation and identify feedback use as an important dimension requiring further pedagogical attention in religious education.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence have contributed to several information-theoretic results through genuinely different modes: a language model may suggest a proof, participate in an extended mathematical dialogue, coordinate computation, or operate as one component of a search harness. Treating all of these as "AI-discovered mathematics" obscures distinctions that matter for scientific reliability, attribution, and reproducibility. This article examines a set of recent cases through a four-stage pipeline: how the problem was formulated; how AI participated in finding a solution; how the resulting analytical and computational claims were verified; and how machine-generated outputs were translated into mathematical exposition for human understanding. Based on these cases, we recommend that research publications (1) disclose the nature and extent of AI assistance at each stage, (2) report verification of analytical reasoning separately from certification of numerical computations, and (3) place more emphasis on articulating the underlying ideas, techniques, and interpretations.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face significant scalability challenges in long-video understanding due to quadratic attention complexity and context window constraints. Existing retrieval-based approaches typically rely on supervised learning from static keyframe annotations. However, these label priors often fail to align with the actual information required by downstream MLLMs for complex reasoning, creating a misalignment between the training target and inference needs. To bridge this gap, we propose a probabilistic framework that reformulates frame selection as latent-variable inference. We first initialize a lightweight policy using supervised learning to capture general visual saliency. Then, we treat a frozen MLLM as a task environment and use its answer likelihood as dense task evidence to refine the policy via Bayesian Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Within this formulation, the negative log-likelihood (NLL) over ground-truth answer tokens provides a principled dense reward, while a prior-matching KL term preserves semantic consistency with the elicited label prior. This process transitions the selection principle from static label priors to task evidence. Extensive experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate that our selector achieves competitive accuracy with MLLM-based scorers while retaining the inference efficiency of lightweight methods. The selector is trained once with a frozen MLLM environment and transfers directly to multiple downstream MLLMs without retraining. Code is available at \url{github.com/Miraclecsc/Frame_Selection_GRPO}.

In this paper, I articulate the transition from my 2025 Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) Postdoctoral Fellowship proposal into an independent, sovereign research lab. The MSCA proposal entitled DUENDE: Decolonial Ubuntu Embodiment for New Dance Epistemologies, was conceptualised as an exploratory research design for a two-year Practice-as-Research (PaR) study at the University of Granada. Its purpose was to propose and test an accessible digital pedagogy for the transcultural transmission of Flamenco in resource-constrained environments. I explain how centering embodiment as my primary epistemology exposed a fundamental tension between institutional grant timelines and the physical limits of the human body. In an era dominated by Large Language Models (LLMs) and hyper-accelerated "Fast Science," somatic integration, habitus, and tissue memory operate on an un-hurried, non-linear tempo. By depositing a summaries of the MSCA proposal methodology, workplan, and flow diagram on on Zenodo as an open-access research blueprint, I pivot away from administrative grant structures to launch the Ubuntu Duende Lab (fea-udl). Grounded in daily living practice, Substack peer-review (@kitaraflamenca), and low-bandwidth digital tools subverted for sovereign pedagogy, this paper establishes an autonomous research framework designed to unfold at the intrinsic speed of the body.

In many human-AI systems, candidate actions are not executed directly but are first evaluated by another decision-making entity under a potentially different objective or decision model. Standard decision-theoretic frameworks do not require this interaction to be represented explicitly, as they define transition dynamics directly over state-action pairs, allowing evaluation to be absorbed within the transition model. We introduce a semantics-aware decision framework in which a candidate action is proposed, evaluated under an interaction context, and then resolved into an executed outcome. We formalize this through a joint action language and an interpretation function that maps each joint action and context to a semantic outcome. Transition and reward dynamics are induced through these semantic outcomes, thereby introducing an explicit representational layer for interaction semantics. Semantic outcomes provide explicit units for organizing interaction principles, which can be instantiated through application-specific evaluation mechanisms and reused across distinct interaction instances. This provides a structured interface for specifying context-dependent evaluation separately from the resulting execution dynamics, without requiring changes to the underlying planning algorithm. We instantiate the framework in shared human-AI autonomy, capturing interaction patterns such as advisory and authorization, and illustrating how interaction context influences decision making. The resulting formulation remains compatible with standard Markov decision process (MDP) planning.

Version 1.00 This essay develops a conceptual framework for the emerging infrastructure of an AI civilization, starting from a concrete real-world incident involving AI agents acting on public wikis. Using the metaphors of a traffic accident and of agents entering another party’s digital property, it derives step by step a set of practical requirements: agent identification, a responsibility address, run or session identity, respect for local rules, incident reconstruction, liability, insurance, certification, and shared responsibility across operators, platforms, model providers, and other actors. The essay does not propose a complete regulatory system. Its method is deliberately incremental: introduce only what becomes necessary from the next concrete problem, and allow institutions and standards to evolve from practice. An accompanying appendix maps these ideas to parallel work already under way in research, standardisation, regulation, and industry, including agent identity, delegation, auditability, incident reporting, insurance, certification, and machine-readable website policies. The central proposal is not a new theory of AI governance, but a way of seeing how already emerging pieces may fit into a broader topology of relationships among actors, spaces, permissions, actions, damage, responsibility, and institutions.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) can improve reasoning in large language models, but specialized non-English domains expose a data mismatch. Raw English domain text is often available, while target-language RLVR tasks with verifiable rewards are scarce. We introduce code-switched task synthesis for cross-lingual RLVR, a data-centric approach that derives target-language and code-switched RLVR task variants from otherwise unverifiable English domain text. Using fill-in-the-middle multiple-choice QA as a seed task format, we synthesize automatically verifiable tasks from domain passages and reshape them into cross-lingual variants. These variants preserve the same evidence-answer relation but change how English and target-language evidence are presented during RLVR. On Korean medical benchmarks and cybersecurity benchmarks across four target languages, code-switched training outperforms matched monolingual and bilingual-mixture baselines on average target-language performance while maintaining comparable English performance. Additional analyses provide evidence of better target-language input understanding and stronger cross-lingual alignment in both model outputs and internal representations. These results suggest that code-switched training helps target-language inputs access domain reasoning learned more strongly in English.

Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are becoming a powerful alternative to conventional tabular learning, adapting to new datasets in context without task-specific training. Current architectures, however, face a trade-off: models that preserve cell-level representations are expensive because they repeatedly attend across rows and columns, while faster models collapse each row into a fixed embedding and lose this fine-grained state. We introduce Factorized Tabular Foundation Models (FTFM), which preserve cell representations while factorizing their computation through one contextual latent per row and one per column. Cells no longer attend to one another directly; instead, each cell is updated through the interaction of its row and column latents, reducing repeated attention while retaining feature-specific information. FTFM achieves competitive predictive performance in tabular classification on major benchmarks such as TabArena and BeyondArena.

The objective is to determine the effectiveness of a model for developing the professional competencies of students in the energy sector through artificial intelligence-based adaptive learning technologies, to provide a scientific rationale for this model, and to develop the methodological foundations for its implementation within the educational process.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
Innovations in Education and Learning Technologies

documents.abstract: Energy materials development remains experimentally intensive because relevant knowledge is dispersed across heterogeneous sources, material formulas and processing parameters are strongly coupled, and experimental data are often incomplete. Although artificial intelligence (AI), including large language models (LLMs), can support knowledge extraction, materials design, experiment planning and data analysis, these capabilities often operate as isolated tools rather than as a computational–experimental loop. This Perspective proposes a conceptual 4E framework—comprising Extraction, Execution, Evolution, and a Generative AI (GAI) Engine—for energy Materials Intelligence and Manufacturing. Extraction converts literature, experimental records, and multimodal data into structured knowledge. Execution translates encoded recipes into machine-executable protocols for robotic synthesis and characterization while returning real-time feedback. Evolution uses robotic experimental feedback to evaluate a domain-specific Recipe Language Model (RLM), which subsequently recommends new material recipes. The GAI Engine coordinates the RLM, materials database, robotic platform, characterization systems, and digital twin within a closed-loop architecture. The framework is further extended conceptually towards intelligent manufacturing through operational data, process monitoring, quality control, and staged translation from laboratory validation to pilot and industrial operation. The 4E framework therefore provides a pathway, grounded in experimentally demonstrated platforms, that links knowledge, formulas and parameters, robotic execution and feedback-driven learning for Materials Intelligence and Manufacturing.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence has moved from a peripheral tool to a routine feature of student life in higher education.This paper examines how generative AI, and ChatGPT specifically, is used across global and regional student populations, and what challenges accompany that use.Drawing on secondary analysis of four public survey datasets, including a global sample of 23,218 students across 110 countries (Ravšelj et al., 2025) and three available regional datasets from Bangladesh, Colombia, and Ecuador, the study addresses three research questions concerning prevalence and institutional readiness, task level application and regional variation, and the ethical and institutional challenges tied to AI adoption.Results show that 71.4% of the global sample had used ChatGPT, primarily for brainstorming, summarizing, and research assistance, though usage intensity and institutional policy awareness varied meaningfully by region.The three regional datasets converge on a common theme even though each measure it differently: a substantial share of students report reduced verification behavior and self-perceived overreliance on AI tools, a pattern this paper terms experienced dependency to distinguish it from the abstract ethical concern measured by the global dataset.The paper argues that adoption, ethical concern, and experienced dependency function as related but distinct dimensions rather than opposite poles of a single spectrum, and that institutions should track them independently.Implications for policy, faculty development, and future research are discussed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has moved within a few years from experimental tool to routine instrument in marketing departments, and the academic literature is still catching up with that speed. This chapter offers a structured review of work published between 2020 and 2026 on how GenAI is used in marketing, how consumers respond to it, and which governance questions follow. Drawing on journal articles from marketing, information systems, economics and law, together with regulatory documents from the European Union and Türkiye, the chapter first separates predictive from generative systems and maps their uses in content production, personalization, customer interaction and marketing research. It then organizes the consumer evidence around three recurring themes: task-dependent preference for machine advice, authenticity penalties attached to perceived AI authorship, and the ambiguous effects of humanlike design in service encounters. Field and experimental studies of workplace use point to productivity gains that are uneven across workers, while creativity research shows a tension between individual output quality and collective diversity. The chapter also discusses hallucination, representational bias, privacy and dark patterns, the energy demand of large models, and the transparency duties introduced by the EU Artificial Intelligence Act alongside Turkish data protection guidance. Much of the evidence rests on short online experiments and on firms in North America and Europe, so conclusions about long-term behavior and about Türkiye remain provisional. The chapter closes with a research agenda on longitudinal field designs, disclosure formats, cross-cultural replication and the measurement of environmental cost in marketing operations. For managers, the evidence suggests that the source, tone and disclosure of generated content matter as much as its quality.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Digital labour platforms have revolutionised the nature of work by allowing people to offer transportation, delivery, domestic and professional services through technology-based intermediaries. While platform-based work is flexible and provides opportunities for income generation, it also poses serious legal issues relating to the classification of work, social security, fair compensation, occupational safety and the allocation of responsibility among the worker, the platform and the State. The central problem is that platforms often label workers as independent contractors while exercising significant control over the workers’ access to work, pricing, performance measurement and continued participation through algorithmic systems. This leaves a gap between the formal categorisation of workers and the economic nature of the working relationship. This paper explores the connection between worker classification and social security, focusing on the changing landscape of labour law in India. It examines the Code on Social Security, 2020, which recognises gig workers and platform workers, and assesses the extent to which the statutory framework is sufficient to address their vulnerability. It also considers the constitutional concepts of equality, dignity and social justice, the judicial history of employment classification, and international approaches such as those of the United Kingdom and the United States. The study is doctrinal and comparative, drawing on legislation, judicial decisions, government reports, international standards and academic literature. The paper concludes that the recognition of gig and platform workers as separate statutory categories is a significant step, but not sufficient to ensure effective social protection or to resolve the question of employment status. A classification system that is largely contractual and based on labels may allow platforms to evade responsibility for what they actually control. The paper therefore proposes a functional, multi-factor classification test, portable social security benefits, transparent algorithmic management, fair contribution-sharing and accessible dispute-resolution mechanisms. It concludes that India needs a worker-centred regulatory regime that allows for genuine flexibility without shifting undue economic risk onto workers.

In serverless LLM inference, cloud providers commonly locate multiple instances on a single GPU to improve utilization. However, each instance independently maintains its model weights and runtime state, making duplicate GPU memory the primary bottleneck. Memory deduplication is a widely-used technique for eliminating duplicate data in CPU systems, but extending it to GPU memory faces fundamental challenges. Effective GPU memory deduplication must avoid redundant data movement between CPU and GPU while preserving write isolation for shared pages without native copy-on-write (COW) support. This paper presents gKSM, a transparent GPU memory deduplication framework for serverless LLM inference. gKSM addresses these challenges through CPU-GPU collaborative hash management that offloads hash computation to GPU kernels, zero-copy model weight deduplication that eliminates duplication before model weight transfer, and a cross-privilege page fault handler that combines a lightweight kernel hook and CUDA Virtual Memory Management (VMM) remapping in the user space. gKSM also designs a stable page scanning algorithm and a reuse-aware placement policy in cluster scale. Experiments show that gKSM reduces GPU memory usage by 59.8% while maintaining high throughput compared to ServerlessLLM. Under memory constrained workloads, gKSM improves aggregate throughput by 2.15X and supports five instances concurrently. In cluster level simulation, gKSM achieves a service rate of 99.97%, compared to 78.2% for SLInfer and 26.9% for ServerlessLLM.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have emerged as transformative technologies in pharmaceutical research, significantly influencing the design, optimization, and personalization of drug delivery systems.AI-assisted approaches are increasingly applied to predict drug release kinetics, optimize formulation parameters, identify novel drug carriers, enhance therapeutic efficacy, and accelerate pharmaceutical product development.Despite the rapid growth of this interdisciplinary research area, a comprehensive understanding of its global scientific evolution, collaborative networks, and emerging research themes remains limited.The present study aims to systematically map the global research landscape of AI and ML applications in drug delivery technology through a bibliometric analysis of publications published between 2015 and 2026.Bibliographic records will be retrieved from the Scopus database using a predefined search strategy, screened according to established inclusion and exclusion criteria, and analyzed using Bibliometrix (R-package) and VOSviewer.The study will evaluate annual publication trends, citation performance, influential authors, institutions, countries, journals, collaborative networks, keyword co-occurrence, thematic evolution, and emerging research hotspots.The findings are expected to provide a comprehensive overview of the intellectual structure and development of AI-driven drug delivery research, identify influential contributors and collaborative patterns, and highlight promising directions for future investigations.The study also seeks to offer practical insights for researchers, pharmaceutical scientists, healthcare professionals, policymakers, and industry stakeholders by identifying technological innovations that can enhance drug development processes and improve patient-centric therapeutic outcomes.By integrating bibliometric techniques with science mapping, this study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on AI-enabled pharmaceutical technologies and provides a strategic research agenda for advancing intelligent drug delivery systems.

Digital health technologies, including mobile applications, clinical decision-support systems, software-based medical technologies and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled tools, are increasingly integrated into healthcare delivery. Within the UK National Health Service (NHS), these technologies offer opportunities to improve patient outcomes, operational efficiency and data-driven clinical decision-making. Their implementation, however, introduces complex challenges relating to medical device qualification and classification, clinical safety, cybersecurity, interoperability, data governance and regulatory compliance.This study examines the regulatory and governance frameworks applicable to AI-enabled digital health and medical device systems within the NHS, with particular emphasis on the Clinical Risk Management Standards DCB0129 and DCB0160, the Digital Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC), and relevant UK medical device regulatory requirements. A structured literature review was conducted using PubMed, covering publications between 2015 and 2025. Sixty studies were included and analysed using a narrative synthesis approach to identify recurring regulatory, technical and governance challenges associated with the implementation and lifecycle management of digital health technologies.The findings indicate that existing NHS frameworks provide an important foundation for clinical safety, data protection, cybersecurity and organisational assurance. However, their application becomes increasingly complex for interconnected and adaptive AI-enabled systems. Key challenges include uncertainty in medical device qualification and regulatory classification, fragmentation across governance requirements, algorithmic bias and explainability, data integrity, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, interoperability, limitations in conventional evaluation approaches, and the need for continuous monitoring of system performance following implementation.Drawing on these findings, this study proposes a Unified NHS AI Governance and Compliance Model that integrates medical device qualification and regulatory classification with clinical safety, data protection, cybersecurity, usability and accessibility, interoperability, and data and AI workflow governance. The model provides a structured lifecycle approach to support early determination of regulatory requirements, clearer allocation of organisational responsibilities, proportionate risk assessment, implementation assurance and post-deployment monitoring.The study concludes that governance of AI-enabled digital health and medical device technologies should evolve towards a more integrated, adaptive and risk-based approach that aligns medical device regulation with wider digital-health assurance requirements. Although developed within the NHS context, the proposed framework may provide a transferable governance approach for healthcare organisations implementing complex, interoperable and AI-enabled digital technologies.
