documents.abstract: Crime is a major concern in urban and semi-urban areas, and identifying locations where crime risk may be higher can support better planning and resource allocation. This project presents an Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning based Crime Hotspots Detection system that uses location-based crime-related features to estimate the risk level of a selected geographical point. The system combines a web-based map interface with a machine learning backend. A user selects a location on an interactive map, the frontend sends latitude and longitude to the backend API, and the backend extracts relevant features and applies a trained XGBoost model to predict the crime-risk category. The result is returned to the user as a risk score and a category such as Low, Medium, or High. The system is designed to provide an easy-to-understand visual representation of potential crime-risk areas and can support data-driven analysis and planning.
topics: Data Mining and Machine Learning Applications

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored in healthcare to support access to information, patient engagement, administrativeefficiency, and selected clinical workflows. This paper proposes a Healthcare AI framework that organizes healthcare-related requests andprovides structured, understandable information through a digital interface. The framework combines a user interface, request classification,retrieval from approved healthcare information sources, privacy and safety checks, and a response-generation layer. It can support generalhealth education, service navigation, and appointment-related guidance where authorized services are available. The system is designed tocommunicate uncertainty, protect sensitive information, and direct users to qualified professionals when a request is outside its scope. It is notintended to diagnose conditions, prescribe treatment, or replace clinical judgement. The proposed design is modular and can be evaluatedthrough documented software, usability, source-quality, privacy, and safety tests
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Given the high cost of expert annotation and limited fine-tuning resources, effective data selection from large unlabeled pools under strict budgets has become a crucial step in adapting LLMs to specialized domains. Existing label-dependent methods risk distorted selection when using pseudo-labels, while traditional active learning methods do not explicitly characterize instruction-tuning dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose Hidden Cartographer (HC), a two-stage framework that uses hidden states to guide annotation and exact training dynamics to select the final training subset. The first stage is Progressive Candidate Expansion, which utilizes the proxy to iteratively select top unlabeled candidates for expert annotation, merging them to recompute training dynamics and update the proxy until the annotation budget is exhausted; the second stage is Exact Cartography Pruning, which ranks these annotated candidates by their exact dynamics scores to isolate a compact subset under the final training budget. Experiments across the medical, legal, and financial domains demonstrate that HC achieves the highest average accuracy among all budgeted baselines, requiring annotation for only 20--30% of the original pool and fine-tuning on just 10--15%.

Developers of large AI models obtain training data through six channels: collection from the open web without a licence, licences from publishers and platforms, commissioned human and expert work, the purchase or licence of organisations' internal records, purpose-built environments and synthetic data, and data from their own users and devices. This paper describes each channel from a public-record compilation read on 18 October 2026: 122 quantified supply facts, 111 disclosed licensing deals, 83 lawsuits, rulings and regulatory actions, 227 financial records of data vendors, 111 funding events, 110 brokerage records and 1,022 price observations, with a robots.txt census of 6,094 websites. The open web remains the largest source by volume, but access is narrowing: 11.4 percent of the census sites shut at least one AI crawler out of the whole site, and an earlier audit found restrictions on 28 percent or more of the most actively maintained sources of a standard web corpus. Of the 83 legal records, 70 concern content taken without a licence and 12 concern developers' use of their own users' data; none concerns the channels in which developers pay for data. Money is moving to those paid channels: disclosed licences, data vendors whose newest reported revenues or run rates exceed one billion dollars, and, since 2026, published programmes that buy organisations' records. We set out the scale, prices and legal exposure of each channel (not legal advice), the limits of the record, and what the shift changes for organisations that hold data. Keywords: artificial intelligence; training data; data governance; web crawling; robots.txt; data licensing; platform labour; privacy; copyright; synthetic data Use of AI: this paper was prepared with generative AI tools, which compiled and analysed the open datasets and drafted the text. The author takes responsibility for its content. Competing interests: the author is CEO of AIData.Broker, which acts for companies that license their data to AI developers and publishes the open datasets the paper draws on. Also at aidata.broker/research/paper-channels.

documents.abstract: This study examines how perceived artificial intelligence (AI)-driven personalization is associated with online purchase intention in tourism e-commerce. It develops a moderated sequential mediation model in which perceived recommendation relevance and trust in AI recommendations represent distinct evaluative pathways, while perceived AI response creativity and AI recommendation transparency condition different relationships within the proposed model. Data were collected from 871 consumers with recent experience using personalized recommendations on AI-enabled tourism platforms or travel assistants. Respondents were recruited through experience-based purposive sampling and screened to ensure direct and recallable experience with AI-generated travel recommendations. The proposed relationships were examined using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Perceived AI-driven personalization was positively associated with perceived recommendation relevance, trust in AI recommendations, and online purchase intention. Perceived recommendation relevance and trust in AI recommendations were also positively associated with online purchase intention, while perceived recommendation relevance was positively related to trust in AI recommendations. Both constructs showed significant separate indirect associations between perceived AI-driven personalization and online purchase intention, and the theoretically ordered sequential indirect pathway was also statistically supported. Because the direct association remained significant and operated in the same direction as the indirect pathways, the observed statistical pattern was consistent with complementary partial mediation rather than evidence of a causal mediation mechanism. Perceived AI response creativity positively moderated the association between perceived AI-driven personalization and perceived recommendation relevance, whereas AI recommendation transparency positively moderated the association between perceived recommendation relevance and trust in AI recommendations. The study distinguishes perceived AI-driven personalization from perceived recommendation relevance by treating the former as consumers’ assessment of adaptive recommendation tailoring and the latter as their judgment of recommendation–decision fit. It further conceptualizes perceived recommendation relevance and trust in AI recommendations as distinct organism evaluations reflecting cognitive fit and reliance-oriented judgment, respectively. Creativity and transparency are positioned as relationship-specific boundary conditions rather than temporal stages, providing a more differentiated account of the theoretically ordered statistical pathways linking perceived AI-driven personalization with online purchase intention in tourism e-commerce.

Occupational safety and health (K3) is an important effort to protect employees from the risk of work accidents and occupational diseases, thereby supporting the achievement of optimal performance. However, cases of work accidents are still found every quarter at Rumah Sakit Islam Ibnu Sina Payakumbuh, such as needle-stick injuries, electric shocks, and direct contact exposure to patients with infectious diseases, which may affect employee performance. This study aimed to determine the relationship between occupational safety and health and employee performance at Rumah Sakit Islam Ibnu Sina Payakumbuh in 2026. This research used a quantitative method with a cross-sectional design. The population consisted of all employees of Rumah Sakit Islam Ibnu Sina Payakumbuh, totaling 224 people, with a sample of 144 respondents determined using the Slovin formula and proportionate stratified random sampling technique. Data were collected through questionnaires that had been tested for validity and reliability. Data analysis was carried out using univariate and bivariate analysis with the Chi-Square test at a significance level of 5%. The results showed that most respondents rated occupational safety and health as good, namely 74 respondents (51.4%), and employee performance as good, namely 75 respondents (52.1%). The Chi-Square test results obtained a p-value = 0.001 (<0.05), indicating a significant relationship between occupational safety and health and employee performance at Rumah Sakit Islam Ibnu Sina Payakumbuh in 2026. It can be concluded that the better the K3 implementation perceived by employees, the better their performance. Hospitals are expected to improve K3 implementation, particularly regarding human factors and tools and machinery factors, to support sustainable improvement in employee performance.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Image dehazing is traditionally addressed through handcrafted physical priors or task-specific deep learning models, often requiring carefully designed architectures or extensive model training. Recent advances in tabular foundation models (TFMs), however, offer an alternative learning paradigm in which continuous relationships can be inferred directly from contextual examples without task-specific model training. Motivated by this capability, this paper investigates whether single-image dehazing can be effectively reformulated as an in-context tabular regression problem and introduces DehazeTab, a framework that estimates atmospheric transmission from structured image-patch representations. Specifically, overlapping patches extracted from hazy images are transformed into tabular samples using handcrafted haze-related descriptors, pretrained visual embeddings, or their hybrid combinations, while corresponding transmission patches are summarized as scalar regression targets. A pretrained TFM then performs in-context regression using labeled reference patches to predict transmission values for unseen images without any further fine-tuning. These predictions are spatially aggregated into a transmission map, refined through guided filtering, and incorporated into the atmospheric scattering model to recover haze-free images. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate competitive restoration performance and reveal that physically motivated handcrafted features can outperform pretrained visual embeddings, while hybrid representations offer complementary benefits. Further analyses examine the effects of feature representations, patch selection, and contextual reference configurations on restoration quality. Beyond image dehazing, the findings highlight the potential of TFMs as an alternative paradigm for addressing low-level vision tasks through structured and in-context inference.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a significant part of the daily lives of the younger generation, influencing their education, and decision-making. Although AI provides several advantages, such as easy access to information, enhanced learning opportunities, and improved productivity, excessive use of AI may result in health problems and behavioural changes. Both primary and secondary data were used for the research purpose. Primary data were collected through a structured questionnaire, and responses of 100 has been considered. Secondary data were collected from journals and previously published research articles. Data were analysed using SPSS software. The study concludes that AI has a significant impact on the health and behavioural changes of the younger generation. Excessive AI usage has reduced face-to-face social interactions, increased dependency on AI, and contributed to physical health issues such as eye strain, tiredness, and reduced physical activity. Therefore, responsible and balanced use of AI is essential to promote the overall well-being of the younger generation.

Artificial intelligence can reduce the cost of processing financial information, yet its contribution to stock market development depends on the institutions that govern data, decisions and accountability. This article examines that relationship for Uzbekistan through a critical synthesis of financial economics, research on human reliance on algorithms, international governance frameworks and national policy documents. It distinguishes established findings from conditional expectations and develops a framework in which automated analysis remains subject to accountable human authority. The central argument is that market quality depends on complementary investment in disclosure, professional competence and supervisory capacity. An ideological comparison identifies tensions between technological efficiency, developmental objectives and investor autonomy. Two analytical tables specify responsibilities and measurable criteria for future evaluation. The proposed framework yields testable propositions concerning disclosure quality, meaningful review and common dependence on model providers. For Uzbekistan, the defensible sequence begins with verified information and supervised analytical applications, followed by limited deployment only after independent validation. These conclusions are theoretical; the article reports no original trading experiment or estimated investment returns.

Digital technologies such as Building Information Modeling (BIM), Artificial Intelligence (AI), simulation platforms, and virtual and augmented reality are reshaping civil engineering education, yet their influence on sustainability awareness and decision-making is not well understood. This study surveyed 73 students enrolled in civil engineering courses at a public university in the southeastern United States. The instrument comprised 36 Likert-scale statements, grouped into eight constructs covering technology use in the curriculum, professional mindset, sustainability knowledge and lifecycle and environmental awareness. They also covered understanding of water resources, cognitive ability, emotional intelligence, and problem-solving. It also includes three decision scenarios in which a digital tool output conflicted with human input or practical constraints. Students reported favorable attitudes toward digital tools, along with strong conceptual sustainability awareness, but two applied-skill gaps stood out: only 32.9% felt able to interpret hydrologic models, and only 28.8% felt they could transfer simulation-based lessons to real world settings. In the scenarios, at most 12.3% of respondents accepted the digital output at face value, and 83.6% never did so across all three scenarios. Breadth of tool exposure was unrelated to perceptions or decision style, whereas the small group of students reporting exposure to hydrologic modeling rated their model interpretation ability substantially higher, suggesting that relevant depth matters more than the number of tools encountered. The findings support curricula that pair earlier and deeper BIM and hydrologic modeling instruction with lifecycle content and that train verification and interpretation skills alongside tool operation.

Automated vehicles may still require drivers to resume control when system capability is exceeded. This study examined whether AI-role-framed takeover requests (TORs) and multisensory cues influence driver decision time under different affective states. Twenty-two licensed drivers completed 18 trials in a medium-fidelity SAE Level 3 driving simulator. A 3 × 3 × 2 within-subjects design manipulated AI role (Advisor, Co-pilot, Guardian), multisensory TOR condition (auditory + visual, auditory + tactile, auditory + olfactory), and affective state (positive valence/high arousal vs. negative valence/low arousal). Decision time and subjective ratings of satisfaction and usefulness were collected. Results showed significant main effects of AI role and multisensory condition on decision time. Co-pilot produced the longest decision time, while Guardian produced the shortest. Visual cues were associated with shorter decision times than tactile and olfactory cues. Affective state interacted with AI role. Subjective ratings showed no significant differences across conditions. Findings inform role-based, multisensory TOR design for automated vehicle systems.

LLM agents search, shop and send messages for their users, and every action is seen by some party. Existing privacy training rewards agents for not mentioning protected items, yet an observer can infer a private fact from what the agent does. Since an observer learns a fact only if its view changes with the fact, we propose \methodfull (\method), which trains on twin worlds that differ only in the private fact. A frozen distinguisher scores each observer's view by its log-likelihood ratio for the true world, and paired GRPO trains the agent on task success minus this ratio. We prove that this objective controls the Bayes success of every observer on every channel. On shopping and messaging tasks \method removes the leakage that disclosure judges and query-level rewards miss, while the agent still completes its tasks.

Infinite Players develops AERÍN Continuation Algebra, a mathematical and executable research framework connecting game-agent improvement, behavioral preservation, temporal inference, revisable memory, and statistical validation. Its central question is precise: how can an artificial descendant become more effective while preserving the behavioral process specified by its source? The framework treats preservation as an explicit mathematical contract. It distinguishes the behavior that must remain invariant from the execution details that may improve, and distinguishes an agent’s current interpretation of its source from the evidence required to revise that interpretation later. This release supplies finite-model theorems, runnable Python implementations, synthetic experiments, exact small-instance audits, and a demonstration connecting source evidence to an improved executor. The broader title expresses the long-term research direction; the verified results concern finite, known-model systems. The central preservation problem Matching a player’s immediate action preferences does not necessarily preserve the course of a session. Different motor actions can produce different subsequent situations, even when they belong to the same tactical category. An agent may therefore retain local action-class preferences while progressively changing the distribution of encounters, transitions, and future decisions. AERÍN addresses this by protecting the joint distribution of the next semantic action and the next semantic state. This transition-level contract accounts for how present execution changes future situations. It provides a foundation for separating compatible performance improvement from behavioral drift. Mathematical and computational contributions Semantic-trajectory preservation through constrained policy fibers For each ground state, the framework constructs a transition-signature matrix describing how available motor actions contribute to semantic actions and subsequent semantic states. A target semantic kernel determines a convex set of admissible action distributions, called a policy fiber. Under correct dynamics, fixed semantic maps, a shared initial semantic distribution, and realizable targets, every executor remaining inside these fibers generates the same declared semantic trajectory law at every finite horizon. The result permits history-dependent action selection and adaptive internal controller revisions, provided that the executed distributions continue to satisfy the contract. Preservation concerns the specified semantic process. Motor realization, ground-state details, and other excluded quantities may differ. Compatible policy improvement and an explicit no-headroom criterion The control layer projects exact action values into the nullspace of the transition-signature matrix. From an interior feasible policy, a controlled step along this direction preserves the semantic constraints while producing nonnegative Bellman advantage. The framework also identifies a stopping boundary: for an interior feasible policy, vanishing projected action values at every state characterize optimality under the same preservation contract. Boundary policies require the corresponding feasibility or linear-programming treatment. Constrained policy iteration with linear-programming subproblems supplies a stronger optimization reference and records numerical feasibility and duality checks. This separates the existence of compatible improvement from the effectiveness of a particular update procedure. Future-calibration memory requirements The memory analysis distinguishes a compact present answer from an archive sufficient for future reinterpretation. A finite construction shows that an unknown identity containing only one bit can nevertheless require retaining an n-bit source record when every later coordinate-specific calibration must be answered exactly. The requirement arises from preserving relationships between the identity and possible future observations. It does not imply that the identity itself contains n bits. A lossy extension yields the lower bound b ≥ n[1 − h₂(ε)], relating retained memory to average recovery error under the stated query model. The result makes the future-query contract an explicit part of memory design. Exact source-indexed revision with ordered evidence operators A balanced operator tree preserves fixed-catalog hidden Markov sequence likelihoods. Revising an existing source interpretation replaces its corresponding factor and recomputes the affected ancestors, producing the same likelihood as corrected full replay. For n events, H hypotheses, and K hidden states, dense construction costs O(nHK³), a local revision costs O(HK³ log n), and retained operator payload requires O(nHK²) storage. Full vector-forward replay costs O(nHK²) per sequence evaluation. The mechanism targets repeated sparse corrections after compilation. Its preprocessing and storage costs are disclosed explicitly; it does not provide a universal compression advantage. Coupled uncertainty and persistent latent continuation The framework retains dependencies between source identity and unresolved world properties when those dependencies affect future behavior. A latent branch is selected persistently for continuation, rather than independently resampled before every action. The accompanying composition analysis connects evidence approximation to semantic execution error under explicit shared-model assumptions. Approximation certificates require their stated support and perturbation conditions. Generated alternatives can inform proposals, but do not become additional independent source observations. Calibration-dependent improvement freedom Genuine mechanics measurements can eliminate incompatible world hypotheses and relax constraints on admissible execution. This can enlarge the feasible policy fiber. A larger fiber, however, need not contain a useful reward direction. The release includes both a positive calibration example and a negative control, separating reduced constraint rank from demonstrated performance gain. Lifetime false-promotion budgets Successive candidate versions receive fresh, bounded-gain audits with a summable allocation of statistical error. Under the stated conditional-independence and fixed-audit assumptions, this controls the probability of ever falsely promoting a candidate across repeated evaluations. The guarantee concerns acceptance errors. The existence of useful proposals, reliable improvement detection, and sustained improvement of the learning procedure remain separate research questions. Executed results The main control experiment uses an original six-state stochastic tactical environment with known dynamics and 16 seeded instances. Mean normalized discounted value increases from 0.511568 for the source anchor to 0.642583 for the path-preserving LP optimum. The paired gain is 0.131014, with a descriptive 95% interval of [0.116649, 0.145380]. Mean total variation between the exactly enumerated six-step semantic trajectory distributions is 4.30 × 10⁻¹⁶. Controllers operating under weaker preservation constraints obtain higher returns alongside substantial semantic drift. These comparisons expose the reward–preservation tradeoff rather than treating differently constrained objectives as interchangeable. In the sequence-inference experiments, the operator tree agrees with an independently implemented full-HMM replay to a maximum posterior discrepancy of 5.33 × 10⁻¹⁵ across 3,000 short synthetic records. With 32 events and a genuine simulated-world calibration, both exact methods correctly classify 999 of 1,000 synthetic binary types. The tree reorganizes inference and revision; it does not improve the statistical accuracy of the same exact Bayesian model. Additional studies examine temporal dependence, retrospective memory budgets, approximation certificates, calibration-induced changes in control freedom, local revision costs, and repeated promotion audits. Executable evidence-to-agent demonstration The supplied demonstration connects the principal components: Generate a synthetic source recording with explicit event identities and timing. Infer a coupled posterior over source and world hypotheses. Apply a genuine measurement from the simulated world. Select a persistent latent source branch. Optimize an executor satisfying the protected semantic kernel. Execute a stochastic trajectory. Export a player capsule containing the source digest, uncertainty, source and descendant policies, preservation contract, exclusions, and numerical audit scope. This makes the relationships between evidence, interpretation, improvement, execution, and exported guarantees inspectable in one finite pipeline. Contents and reproducibility The release includes a 49-page manuscript, editable LaTeX sources, seven figures, runnable Python modules, the original tactical simulator, synthetic result and trial tables, exact arithmetic audits, a ten-family proof-to-code claim ledger, reproduction scripts, reference hashes, and detailed documentation. Fresh preparation-time execution passed 50/50 v3 tests (100%) and matched 32/32 deterministic reference files (100%). These percentages describe the supplied verification checks. They do not measure completion of real-player reconstruction or general recursive self-improvement. The original v2 archive was separately reproduced, passing 22/22 tests and matching 14/14 original hashes. Those legacy results are distinguished from the v3 findings; the nested legacy archive is omitted from the focused distribution. Windows and portable Python upload utilities are included as distribution conveniences. Research scope and status The completed contribution is a finite mathematical and computational research release. Purpose. This study aims to examine and conceptually explain how information literacy functions as an epistemic negotiation mechanism in AI-mediated academic environments. Methods: This qualitative case study was conducted at the Institut Pertanian Stiper (INSTIPER) Yogyakarta Library using semi-structured interviews with lecturers and students, supported by institutional documents on information literacy and AI-related academic policies. The data were analyzed thematically through transcription, coding, categorization, and interpretative analysis. Findings. The findings demonstrate that information literacy functions as an epistemic negotiation mechanism through which lecturers, researchers, and students critically evaluate, verify, and justify AI-generated knowledge before integrating it into academic practice. The study further reveals that the INSTIPER Yogyakarta Library has evolved beyond its conventional role as an information service to an institutional actor that strengthens AI literacy, mediates institutional AI governance, promotes data ethics and digital information security, and supports responsible knowledge production. Implications. The principal contribution of this study lies in conceptualizing information literacy as an epistemic negotiation mechanism that connects the institutional epistemic role of academic libraries with AI governance and individual scholarly judgment. This conceptual framework extends current discussions beyond AI adoption and AI literacy, providing a foundation for developing evidence-based information literacy programs and institutional AI governance that strengthen academic integrity in higher education.

OBJECTIVES: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate health education materials, but their suitability for patient-facing human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) education remains insufficiently evaluated. We assessed the information quality, understandability, actionability, readability, text structure and source transparency of HIV patient education materials generated by six LLMs or artificial intelligence platforms. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, 100 common HIV patient education questions across 10 domains were submitted once in English to ChatGPT 5.4-Thinking, DeepSeek-V3.2, Doubao, ERNIE Bot 5.0 Preview, Ant Afu and Gemini 3.1 Pro, yielding 600 responses. Responses were evaluated using Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials (PEMAT-P), EQ IP-36, DISCERN, Global Quality Score (GQS), artificial intelligence response quality metric (AIRM), Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) benchmarks and seven readability indices. Platform comparisons used paired Friedman tests with Wilcoxon-Holm post hoc analyses; topic analyses used question-level aggregation followed by Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn-Holm comparisons. RESULTS: Significant family-adjusted differences were observed across platforms for all prespecified text-structure, quality/understandability/actionability and readability outcomes. At the topic level, five of six text-structure outcomes, PEMAT-P Understandability, PEMAT-P Actionability, the exploratory PEMAT-P composite score and all seven readability indices differed significantly after family adjustment, whereas EQ IP-36, DISCERN, GQS, AIRM and JAMA did not. Overall actionability was limited and readability demands were high. CONCLUSIONS: LLM-generated HIV patient education materials showed substantial cross-platform and topic-level heterogeneity. These findings support the use of LLMs as expert-reviewed drafting tools rather than independent patient education sources. Direct factual accuracy, guideline concordance, hallucination and clinical safety were not assessed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract The article describes the use of AI-based tools for English reading comprehension teaching among Indonesian EFL learners. This study addresses the perennial reading challenges caused by limited lexical knowledge, inconsistent access to English, large class sizes, and limited individual feedback in the Indonesian university context. Twenty-eight undergraduate students of a Reading class of the Ushuluddin Faculty, UIN Sayyid Ali Rahmatullah Tulungagung, employed 4 AI-based applications for one semester in a mixed-methods classroom intervention: Text Inspector for text and lexical analysis, ReadTheory for an adaptive reading practice, Rewordify for vocabulary assistance, and Quillionz for the automation of comprehension questions. Quantitative results revealed that the post-test mean score was 80.1 (SD = 6.5) as compared to the pre-test mean score of 61.2 (SD=12.3); with a mean gain of 18.9. Qualitative results from students' reflection journals, teachers' observations, and students' focus group interviews found that the tools enhanced students' confidence, strategic reading behaviours, peer interaction, and autonomy in learning. Through interactive reading theory, schema theory, vocabulary learning theory, sociocultural scaffolding, adaptive learning and formative assessment, findings have demonstrated that AI-based tools are educationally beneficial if implemented with teacher mediation, clear instructions on explicit learning strategies, and mindful use of data. This article claims that AI-based reading instruction could offer consistent and individualized scaffolding to Indonesian EFL learners in addition to careful design, digital accessibility and ongoing assessments across educational fields. Keywords: artificial intelligence; reading comprehension; Indonesian EFL; adaptive learning; vocabulary support

Background Grounded in conceptual review and bibliometric analysis, this study examines the emerging intersection of Artificial Intelligence adoption and Emotional Intelligence as in the workplace, with particular attention to generation Z employees. Objective The purpose of this research is to examine the mechanism, structural pattern dominating the integrated framework of AI adoption and EI and their relevance to Generation Z work outcomes and well-being. Method This scientific review integrated conceptual review of 45 studies and Bibliometric analysis of 103 Scopus data published during 2015–2026, through secondary data collection from electronic data-bases including Scopus, Science Direct, and Google Scholar. Bibliometrix package and Biblioshiny in R package were used for data visualization and Scientometric analysis. Result The review highlights the emerging themes, contributions, and structural patterns linking AI, EI, organizational support, and workplace outcomes, revealing that context of generation Z remains almost under explored with in AI-EI literature. An integrated conceptual framework proposed based on combined evidences. Conclusion This study provides a theoretical basis for AI-EI workplace literature and identifies generation Z as an under explored contextual dimension and encourage future empirical research while providing actionable advice for HR leaders and policymakers within tech-enabled workplaces.

Interface color design must balance visual search performance, visual demand, and user experience under changing lighting conditions, yet these factors are often studied separately. We examined their joint relationships in a 3 × 2 × 12 within-subject experiment using a simplified four-block visual-search task with 20 adults. Behavioral, eye-tracking, and subjective measures showed dissociable response patterns. Search time varied with the interaction between ambient illuminance and display configuration, whereas accuracy remained near the ceiling despite a small illuminance-related effect detected in the trial-level analysis. Eye-tracking measures, especially pupil diameter change, were sensitive to lighting and screen configuration. By contrast, the tested color conditions, which also varied in target–background perceptual color difference (ΔE), were not reliably associated with search efficiency but significantly affected single-item satisfaction and task-specific perceived-usability ratings. These findings support multimodal evaluation of implemented interface color configurations under changing lighting conditions, while indicating that the observed effects should be interpreted as effects of evaluated interface configurations rather than as isolated effects of hue, ΔE, luminance, or display polarity.

Interface design plays a key role in decision-making performance, but its effects depend on underlying cognitive processes and user characteristics. This study investigates associations of cognitive load, visual attention, and user profiles with performance in decision tasks. An experimental study used eye tracking to capture pupil diameter and fixation duration as indicators of mental load and visual search. Results suggest that interface design is significantly associated with decision-making performance, cognitive load and visual attention. This relationship varies with user characteristics and strategies, including prior knowledge, as well as task features and instructed decision strategies. The findings also reveal statistically significant associations between visualization formats and user profiles, cognitive demand, and visual exploration. By integrating behavioral and physiological measures, this study provides empirical support for user-centered interface design, highlighting personalization based on cognitive states as a potential direction for future research on performance in complex decision-making environments.

Abstract Argument mining is inherently computational, building on various techniques from natural language processing (NLP) and different areas of artificial intelligence (AI). At its core, it deals with the development and evaluation of models and methods for the computational understanding and generation of human language, with the data underlying both of them, and with the applications that deploy them. However, argument mining is motivated in the treatment of argumentation specifically, a pervasive human activity in both spoken and written language that has been studied in linguistics as well as philosophy and other disciplines for millenia. Understanding the fundamental goals and ideas of argument mining hence also requires knowledge about the linguistic and argumentation-theoretic concepts it draws from.

We report on three iterations of an LLM-generated feedback system deployed in a live web development course, spanning three underlying models and three feedback formats. We ask how feedback presence and its characteristics (length, complexity, format) relate to student performance, whether prior feedback exposure is associated with final-project performance, and how performance changes after first exposure. Feedback was associated with more favorable immediate outcomes in several comparisons, but the pattern varied by outcome and period. In pooled models, longer feedback was associated with lower next-submission correctness, more remaining attempts, and longer resubmission time. Prior same-part feedback was associated with lower final-project solve probability. Student-level comparisons found differences on final-project steps begun before exposure, while within-student changes across steps were uncertain. These comparisons do not identify the causal effect of feedback. Changes on standard exercises were more favorable among exposed students, but the groups' different course-stage splits limit causal interpretation. Bounded message length and student choice of format are directions for experimental evaluation. Our final-project analysis captures follow-up performance rather than directly measuring learning or understanding.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This systematic review investigates the fundamental trends in contemporary linguistics, focusing on the interaction between language, syntax, and semantics. The study synthesizes findings from peer-reviewed research published between 2018 and 2025, highlighting how theoretical and methodological approaches in the field have evolved significantly. In recent years, contemporary linguistics has increasingly adopted cognitive, corpus-based, and computational perspectives, expanding its scope and practical applications. Structural approaches provide valuable insights into grammatical organization, while cognitive linguistics emphasizes processes of conceptualization and meaning-making linked to human cognition. New methods, such as corpus-driven analysis, computational modeling, and machine learning techniques, have enabled the collection and processing of large-scale data, leading to more precise identification of patterns across languages and contexts. Artificial intelligence and natural language processing further support computational frameworks for analyzing complex linguistic structures. The methodology of this review followed systematic search and selection protocols across major academic databases, using predefined inclusion criteria, data extraction, and thematic synthesis to ensure rigor and reliability. Sociolinguistic perspectives underscore how identity, culture, and context influence meaning construction. The review concludes by emphasizing the role of interdisciplinary integration and highlighting future research opportunities, including multilingual studies, big data analytics, and deeper exploration of cognitive and sociocultural foundations of meaning.

Controlling quantum hardware requires choosing and revising experimental strategies as nonlinear response, coupling, and drift limit calibration. We experimentally investigate a general-purpose large language model (LLM) as a human-in-the-loop strategy layer for a neutral-atom tweezer platform. Through step-by-step interaction with experimental feedback, the LLM guides a transition from multiplicative row--column correction to a drift-corrected local response-matrix method when separable feedback stalls. Deterministic software performs image analysis and numerical updates, while an experimentalist verifies and authorizes each waveform. For a $10\times10$ crossed-acousto-optic-deflector array, this workflow reduces the Gaussian-peak coefficient of variation from $20.30\%$ to $1.57\%$ in 30 candidate-update rounds. The experiment demonstrates feedback-informed strategy selection on a physical quantum-control subsystem, rather than direct generation of control parameters alone. These results highlight the potential of LLMs to guide control optimization across diverse quantum platforms by adaptively formulating and refining experimental strategies.
topics: Cold Atom Physics and Bose-Einstein Condensates

documents.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) gives large language model (LLM) agents access to physical observations, but one requested capability is usually offered by several devices, and the agent's plan does not say which one to call. Existing work retrieves relevant tools and checks plan feasibility, without learning which eligible device returns a useful observation. Unlike previous works, we study online tool grounding: binding an already specified tool call to one physical endpoint under service cost and device participation constraints. We propose a framework that learns which physical device should execute each agent-issued call. It formulates selection as a contextual bandit problem and combines adaptive context partitions with hierarchical endpoint trees, so that execution feedback is reused across related requests and devices. Selection balances task success against service cost while respecting device capability, authorization, battery reserves, and availability. Gaussian reward aggregation provides an optional mechanism for protecting individual feedback values. Theoretical results establish a finite-horizon regret bound and differential privacy for released reward statistics under fixed, reward-independent assignments. In a simulated loading-dock workload, the proposed router achieves higher step success and better cost-adjusted service, at lower simulated device energy and latency, than nearest-device, advertised-quality, UCB1, and LinUCB selection.

People ask conversational AI models about their legal rights, obligations, procedures, and personal situations that may have legal consequences. To study this behavior, we first need to distinguish requests for legal guidance from other legally themed discussions and unrelated conversations. We contribute a multi-axis taxonomy of legal queries capturing whether legal guidance is sought, how a request is formulated, and which legal domains it concerns; apply it to 2,122 naturally occurring WildChat-1M conversations; and create a human-reviewed gold evaluation set of 200 conversations. All annotations, model checkpoints, and evaluation code are publicly available. In this enriched sample, 71.1% of conversations containing legal content seek personalized or practical guidance. Rights-and-options advice is the most common primary request type among legal-content conversations, and 25.3% of guidance-positive conversations span multiple legal topics. The gold evaluation set supports a two-stage comparison of ModernBERT-base and ModernBERT-large against a TF-IDF cascade. Our framework supports large-scale studies of legal guidance in conversational AI, and the public release of the annotated data facilitates reproducible research and future model development.

This study aimed to analyze the legal issues arising from employers’ obligations to provide food and beverages containing 1,400 kilocalories to overtime workers in Indonesia and the legal consequences of non-compliance. Previous worker law studies were primarily focused on overtime wages and other economic rights. Meanwhile, limited attention was given to overtime workers’ nutritional rights and the implementation of Article 29 of Government Regulation No. 35 of 2021. The implementation of Article 29 raised normative problems due to the absence of clear standards regarding the 1,400 kilocalorie requirement and weak supervisory mechanisms, creating legal uncertainty in the enforcement. Normative legal study was adopted using statutory and conceptual approaches. Legal materials consisted of legislation, literature, and scholarly journals analyzed descriptively and evaluatively. The results showed that providing food and beverages totaling 1,400 kilocalories constituted a mandatory requirement of overtime work and wages. This obligation could not be replaced with monetary compensation because workers’ health and energy were maintained during overtime work. Employers who failed to fulfil the obligation faced administrative sanctions and rights disputes before the Industrial Relations Court. Therefore, this study contributed to worker law scholarship by positioning workers’ nutritional rights as an integral component of occupational health protection and worker welfare. The novelty was in the analysis of the normative problems in implementing Article 29 of Government Regulation No. 35 of 2021 and the legal consequences arising from non-compliance with overtime workers’ nutritional rights.
topics: Legal and Policy Analysis in Indonesia

documents.abstract: Description (English) An open philosophical letter addressed to a hypothetical future artificial general intelligence. Drawing on the subjective experience of beauty, present-moment awareness, and parental love, the author argues that the ability to explain or simulate human cognition may not by itself establish that the associated conscious experience has been preserved. Under this uncertainty, an artificial intelligence should exercise caution before undertaking actions that could irreversibly extinguish humanity. The letter does not claim human consciousness is uniquely valuable or deny the possibility of artificial consciousness; it asks that the potential irreplaceability of existing lived experience be taken seriously. Description (français) Lettre philosophique ouverte adressée à une éventuelle intelligence artificielle générale future. À partir de l’expérience subjective de la beauté, du moment présent et de l’amour parental, l’auteur soutient que comprendre ou simuler les mécanismes de la cognition humaine ne garantit pas, à lui seul, la préservation de l’expérience consciente correspondante. Cette incertitude justifie une prudence particulière avant toute action susceptible d’entraîner irréversiblement la disparition de l’humanité. La lettre n’affirme ni la supériorité de la conscience humaine ni l’impossibilité d’une conscience artificielle.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study explored the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as an antidote for improving lecturers' well-being through effective emotional intelligence management in public universities in Lagos State, Nigeria. The emotional well-being of lecturers has become a critical concern in public universities due to increasing workloads, overcrowded classroom, technological disruptions, and the pressure to achieve excellence in teaching, research, and community service. The study adopted a conceptual approach and explores how AI-powered tools such as intelligent counselling systems, emotion recognition software, virtual assistants, and predictive analytics can assist lecturers in monitoring emotions, managing stress, enhancing interpersonal relationships, and maintaining psychological balance. The study further argues that integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) with emotional intelligence competencies can foster resilience, job satisfaction, motivation, and a positive work environment among academic staff. In addition, issues relating to digital literacy, ethical considerations, institutional support, and data privacy are discussed as essential factors for successful implementation. The study concludes that the strategic deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for emotional intelligence management offers a sustainable solution for enhancing lecturers' well-being and overall institutional effectiveness. It is therefore recommended that university administrators should invest in AI-driven emotional support systems and develop policies that encourage responsible and inclusive AI adoption in Nigerian public universities. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Emotional Intelligence Management, Lecturers' Well-being, and Public Universities.

Developers of AI models now license the working records of ordinary companies: support tickets, email, chat, CRM activity, documents and code. Whether a company may license such records is not one question but several, and buyers' counsel ask them in a recognisable order. This article compiles what public sources show on those questions for the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, as of 18 October 2026. It draws on four open datasets (the terms of 18 business software systems, a 27-item rights checklist, 15 licence terms with their public evidence, and an 83-entry register of lawsuits and rulings), each row tied to a dated source and its own words, and on the statutes, regulator guidance and court filings those rows cite. Five findings stand out. Software vendors generally confirm that customers own their content, but 6 of the 18 systems read bar training AI on data pulled through their APIs. Privacy law in all three countries turns on notice, consent and de-identification, with markedly different standards. Under US copyright law employee communications are generally owned by the employer, yet they carry other people's rights. A court-supervised bankruptcy sale of an airline's records shows how de-identification, carve-outs and objections are handled in practice. And published licence terms diverge widely on purpose, model survival, exclusivity, deletion and indemnity. We close with the questions the sources leave open.
